boundary_rationale: The narrator opens with Job's name and place, then states his character in a fourfold formula: “That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil” (web:Job.1.1), Hebrew תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר וִירֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע (oshb:Job.1.1) -- the same four-word chain-- a six-word clause carrying the conjunctive waw on the yare-word that is this verse's own; Yahweh echoes the same character portrait twice more with the waw dropped (oshb:Job.1.8, oshb:Job.2.3). The two-word head תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר is the object that actually recurs byte-identically all three times -- sweep: 3 book-wide, byte tier (Job.1.1, Job.1.8, Job.2.3) -- anchoring the narrator's portrait to Yahweh's own repeated commendation. The row continues without any participant or scene change through the census of sons, daughters, and livestock and into the sons' recurring feast cycle, closed by Job's own precautionary sacrifices and the narrator's habitual summary “Job did so continually” (web:Job.1.5). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.1.5 (single-witness), marking a paragraph close immediately before the heavenly-court scene opens.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the wealth catalog from the sacrificial habit was considered, but nothing in the Hebrew marks an internal break inside this unified portrait of Job's piety.
literature_type_guess: prose frame: Job's character portrait and wealth catalog

boundary_rationale: A fresh scene opens with the verse-initial formula וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם (oshb:Job.1.6; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents), recurring at the next two court/disaster scenes), as the sons of God present themselves before Yahweh and “Satan also came among them” (web:Job.1.6); the satan is introduced with the article, הַשָּׂטָ֖ן (oshb:Job.1.6), a definite description carried through the whole frame rather than a proper name. Yahweh's opening question “Where have you come from?” (web:Job.1.7) and his commendation “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil” (web:Job.1.8) are both verse-initial vayomer frames naming Yahweh as speaker; the satan's own answer to Yahweh's opening question sits interior to Job.1.7, before his separate verse-initial vaya'an formula opens the sharper challenge at Job.1.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through the wager and Job's commendation was considered, but the satan's own vaya'an formula marks where his sharper challenge properly begins.
literature_type_guess: heavenly audience: God's sons and satan present together

boundary_rationale: The satan's verse-initial vaya'an formula וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת יְהוָ֖ה (oshb:Job.1.9) opens his challenge, “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (web:Job.1.9), moving through his accusation to the wager formula שְֽׁלַֽח נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ (oshb:Job.1.11), “But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face” (web:Job.1.11; sweep: 2 book-wide, recurring in the second court scene). Yahweh's grant of permission, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don't stretch out your hand” (web:Job.1.12), is followed in the same verse by the satan's departure, וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵעִ֖ם פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה (oshb:Job.1.12), which closes the scene; no fresh scene-opening formula intervenes before this clause, so the row keeps challenge, wager, and exit together as one exchange.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the wager and the permission as two separate rows was weighed, but both belong to the one continuous exchange the satan's challenge formula opens.
literature_type_guess: satan's first challenge: wager to test Job's devotion

boundary_rationale: A second ויהי היום scene-opening formula, וַיְהִ֖י הַיּ֑וֹם (oshb:Job.1.13; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents)), turns the narrative from the court to the sons' and daughters' feast at their oldest brother's house. Four messengers arrive in sequence, the middle two introduced by the matching relay formula ע֣וֹד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר (oshb:Job.1.16) and (oshb:Job.1.17) -- sweep: 2 book-wide for this spelling -- and the fourth by the variant spelling עַ֚ד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֔ר (oshb:Job.1.18; sweep: 1 book-wide, a distinct spelling from the other two and not a ketiv/qere note). Every one of the four reports, including the first, closes on the identical refrain וָֽאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ (oshb:Job.1.15), “I alone have escaped to tell you” (web:Job.1.15) At consonantal/skeleton tier the refrain sweeps 4 book-wide (oshb:Job.1.15, oshb:Job.1.16, oshb:Job.1.17, oshb:Job.1.19); at pointed/byte tier it sweeps 1 (oshb:Job.1.15 alone carries a meteg on its opening word that the other three lack). Naming the tier, the skeleton-level identity still binds all four blows into a single escalating relay rather than four independent reports.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the earliest messenger's report from the three that follow was an option, but the shared escape-refrain binds all four into one relay.
literature_type_guess: disaster relay: four successive messengers and calamities

boundary_rationale: With the final messenger's report finished, the subject shifts to Job himself: “Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped” (web:Job.1.20). His own speech follows, “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh's name” (web:Job.1.21), and the scene closes on the narrator's integrity verdict בְּכָל זֹ֖את (oshb:Job.1.22), “In all this, Job didn't sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing” (web:Job.1.22; sweep: 2 book-wide, recurring after the second affliction). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.1.22 (single-witness), corroborating the close of this opening movement before the second court scene reopens.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Job's mourning posture into the messenger-relay row was possible, but the shift from the messengers' speech to Job's own action marks a new narrative beat.
literature_type_guess: Job's response: mourning posture and integrity maintained

boundary_rationale: The scene-opening formula recurs a third time, וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם (oshb:Job.2.1; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents), its final member), reopening the heavenly court: “Again, on the day when God's sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan came also among them to present himself before Yahweh” (web:Job.2.1). Yahweh's opening question itself changes wording from the first court scene -- אֵ֥י מִזֶּ֖ה תָּבֹ֑א (oshb:Job.2.2) against מֵאַ֣יִן תָּבֹ֑א (oshb:Job.1.7), two distinct interrogative constructions that WEB renders identically (“Where have you come from?”, web:Job.1.7 and web:Job.2.2) -- before his commendation is extended: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil. He still maintains his integrity, although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause” (web:Job.2.3). The clause itself, spliced fresh from Job.2.3's own bytes, reads אִ֣ישׁ תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֣ר מֵרָ֑ע (oshb:Job.2.3); its two-word head תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר is the character formula's third and byte-identical attestation -- skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents) (Job.1.1, Job.1.8, Job.2.3) -- inside a commendation that now opens אֶל עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּוֹב֒ (oshb:Job.2.3), the preposition shifted from עַל עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּ֑וֹב (oshb:Job.1.8), and carrying the added clause about the satan's own incitement that the first court scene did not have.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this row through the satan's second challenge was considered, but his own vaya'an formula opens a distinct speech-turn at Job.2.4.
literature_type_guess: heavenly court reconvened: God's commendation renewed

boundary_rationale: The satan's second vaya'an formula, וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת יְהוָ֖ה (oshb:Job.2.4), opens his reply, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life” (web:Job.2.4), and the wager formula recurs, שְֽׁלַֽח נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ (oshb:Job.2.5), “But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face” (web:Job.2.5; sweep: 2 book-wide). Yahweh's second grant of permission, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life” (web:Job.2.6), is followed in the same verse-initial chain by the satan's departure and, without any intervening scene-opening formula, by the blow itself: וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵאֵ֖ת פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיַּ֤ךְ אֶת אִיּוֹב֙ בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֔ע מִכַּ֥ף רַגְל֖וֹ עד וְעַ֥ד קָדְקֳדֽוֹ (oshb:Job.2.7; the phrase after the departure carries a ketiv/qere pair עד / ועד, 'to' / 'and to', single-witness). Unlike the earlier court scene, where ויהי היום reopens a fresh scene at Job.1.13 after the satan's exit, no such formula separates the departure from the strike here; the row is drawn through the whole verse rather than cut at Job.2.6|Job.2.7, though that earlier-cutting alternative -- matching the earlier court scene's own shape -- is a live rival and is disclosed rather than resolved.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Placing the seam at Job.2.6|Job.2.7 instead, matching the earlier court scene's own pattern, remains a live alternative and is disclosed here rather than resolved.
literature_type_guess: satan's second wager: bodily affliction strike permitted

boundary_rationale: After the strike recorded at the end of Job.2.7, Job himself becomes the acting subject in his own right, apart from the divine court: “He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes” (web:Job.2.8). This shift in subject and setting -- from the divine court to Job alone on the ash heap -- is the clearest participant-based break available at whole-verse grain, since the striking itself is fused to the satan's departure inside Job.2.7 with no scene-opening formula of its own; the rival cut at Job.2.6|Job.2.7 remains disclosed from the row before this one. His wife's provocation follows, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die” (web:Job.2.9), and Job's rebuttal closes the scene with the verdict formula's second and final attestation, בְּכָל זֹ֛את (oshb:Job.2.10), “In all this Job didn't sin with his lips” (web:Job.2.10; sweep: 2 book-wide). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.2.10 (single-witness), corroborating the close before the friends arrive.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Two distinct rivals were weighed for this row's near edge, each on its own ground. Opening at whole-verse Job.2.7 -- matching the earlier court scene's own shape, where Yahweh's permission and the satan's exit close at 1:12 before ויהי היום reopens a fresh scene at 1:13 -- remains a live alternative; it is not excluded because no formula supports it, but because Job.2.7's strike clause is bound to its own exit clause inside one unbroken verse with no mark keyed to either Job.2.6 or Job.2.7 separating them. A narrower rival, splitting Job.2.7 itself between its exit clause וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵאֵ֖ת פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה and its strike clause וַיַּ֤ךְ אֶת אִיּוֹב֙ בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֔ע, is rejected because no fresh formula supports cutting a single verse in half.
literature_type_guess: affliction and wife: Job on ash heap with taunt

boundary_rationale: Job's three friends enter by name, אֱלִיפַ֤ז הַתֵּימָנִי֙ וּבִלְדַּ֣ד הַשּׁוּחִ֔י וְצוֹפַ֖ר הַנַּֽעֲמָתִ֑י (oshb:Job.2.11): Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, “and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him” (web:Job.2.11). Their approach and grief are narrated at web:Job.2.12, “they raised their voices, and wept” before the row closes on the seven-day silent vigil, “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (web:Job.2.13). This unit's closing edge rests on the wordlessness Job.2.13 states outright -- “no one spoke a word to him” -- which is broken precisely at the seam with web:Job.3.1, where the temporal marker אַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן ('after this') reopens Job's own voice, ending the vigil's silence with his extended lament.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading through into Job's lament was considered, but the seven-day silence this row records is broken specifically by the temporal marker that reopens his voice after the vigil.
literature_type_guess: three friends arrive: gathering and seven-day silence

boundary_rationale: The narrator's report that “After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.” (web:Job.3.1) is followed at once by the dialogue-formula “Job answered:” (web:Job.3.2; Hebrew וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר), a doubled introduction to the same speech-act: a mouth-opening idiom (פָּתַ֤ח אִיּוֹב֙ אֶת פִּ֔יהוּ) paired with the vaya'an-formula proper. Both verses stand apart in register from the wholly poetic curse that opens at 3:3, and together they mark the turn from the silence that closes 2:13 (“So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” web:Job.2.13) to Job's own voice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the pair at the Masoretic paragraph break following 3:1 into two one-verse rows, Job.3.1-Job.3.1 and Job.3.2-Job.3.2, honoring that (single-witness) division over the shared introductory function argued here.
literature_type_guess: discourse frame: narrative mouth-opening and dialogue formula

boundary_rationale: The curse proper opens with the jussive incipit “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.” (web:Job.3.3; Hebrew יֹ֣אבַד י֭וֹם, ‘let the day perish’), a form independently swept at 1 occurrence book-wide (sweep: 1 book-wide, byte tier), and runs a chain of day/night imprecations through “because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.” (web:Job.3.10), which closes the chain by giving its motive (the day did not shut the womb). The next verse turns from cursing the day to interrogating Job's own birth, a distinct topic marked at its own opening (the seam at 3:10|3:11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Break the curse chain at 3:6|3:7 was weighed differently from 3:8|3:9: 3:7 does open with a verse-initial presentative, הִנֵּ֤ה הַלַּ֣יְלָה הַ֭הוּא יְהִ֣י גַלְמ֑וּד אַל תָּבֹ֖א רְנָנָ֣ה בֽוֹ (oshb:Job.3.7), a tier-1 signal class in its own right, but it governs the same subject 3:6 has already introduced -- both verses open on 'that night' (הַלַּ֥יְלָה הַהוּא֮ יִקָּחֵ֪ה֫וּ אֹ֥פֶל אַל יִ֭חַדְּ בִּימֵ֣י שָׁנָ֑ה בְּמִסְפַּ֥ר יְ֝רָחִ֗ים אַל יָבֹֽא, oshb:Job.3.6) -- so the presentative resumes the day/night imprecation rather than turning to a new topic, and the chain is kept whole through it. No interrogative, vocative, or formula marks 3:8|3:9.
literature_type_guess: curse strophe: day perish and night imprecation opening

boundary_rationale: “Why didn’t I die from the womb? Why didn’t I give up the spirit when my mother bore me?” (web:Job.3.11; Hebrew לָ֤מָּה לֹּ֣א מֵרֶ֣חֶם אָמ֑וּת) opens a why-not-death interrogative -- the four-word clause itself is a singleton, sweep: 1 book-wide at byte tier. Its opening word לָ֤מָּה recurs pointed and accented identically at only one other verse, oshb:Job.3.20 -- sweep: 2 book-wide, byte tier (Job.3.11, Job.3.20) -- giving this strophe a matching bookend at its far edge, though 3:20's question shares only the opening particle with 3:11's, not the same interrogative content. The unit develops the death-wish through the rest-among-kings and rest-among-prisoners imagery down to “The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master.” (web:Job.3.19), which closes on the small-and-great leveling motif before the topic turns again at 3:20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treat 3:13-3:15 (rest among kings) and 3:16-3:19 (rest among the unborn and the leveled dead) as two separate rows, but neither sub-block opens on a fresh interrogative, vocative, or formula.
literature_type_guess: interrogative strophe: why birth and death's relief sought

boundary_rationale: “Why is light given to him who is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,” (web:Job.3.20; Hebrew לָ֤מָּה יִתֵּ֣ן לְעָמֵ֣ל א֑וֹר) reopens the interrogative with the same pointed form as 3:11 (sweep: 2 book-wide, byte tier), now turned from the wish for death to the question of light and life for the sufferer. The strophe, and Job's whole opening speech, closes at “I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither do I have rest; but trouble comes.” (web:Job.3.26), whose confession of unrest is corroborated (tier-3, single-witness) by the petuchah following that verse; the verse also carries a paseq, but paseq is an intra-verse disjunctive with no encoded position, so it is disclosed as a bare inventory fact rather than treated as edge corroboration. Eliphaz's formula opens fresh at Job.4.1, closing the lament this verse ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extend this row through 4:1 on the ground that the vaya'an formula is itself part of the lament's close, but the formula's speaker token (Eliphaz, not Job) marks a new speech, not a continuation of it.
literature_type_guess: why-light strophe: darkness preferred to light of being

boundary_rationale: “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,” (web:Job.4.1; Hebrew וַ֭יַּעַן אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר) is one member of the book's vaya'an inventory (sweep: 27 book-wide) and, with the spelling הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י, one of three Eliphaz-token vaya'an members (sweep: 3 book-wide), spelling-distinct from the defective הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י opening oshb:Job.22.1 -- the same WEB rendering at web:Job.22.1 ('Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered') erases the distinction, so the orthographic claim is anchored to the Hebrew bytes, not the English witness. The courteous but pointed opening address runs from “If someone ventures to talk with you, will you be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking?” (web:Job.4.2) through the rhetorical question closing “Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ways your hope?” (web:Job.4.6), after which the imperative zkhor na opens a fresh appeal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolate 4:1 as its own one-verse frame row to mirror the treatment given the doubled introduction at 3:1-3:2, but 4:1 carries one formula, not a paired one, and does not warrant the same isolation.
literature_type_guess: Eliphaz opens: formula plus address to Job's former counsel

boundary_rationale: “Remember, now, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?” (web:Job.4.7; Hebrew זְכָר נָ֗א, ‘remember, now’) opens with an imperative topic-turn appealing to observed precedent, a pattern of retribution the strophe illustrates through the lion imagery running to “The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad.” (web:Job.4.11). The following verse drops the generic proverb register for Eliphaz's own personal account (“Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.” web:Job.4.12), a participant shift that marks the far edge of this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Divide the lion imagery of 4:10-4:11 from the retribution proverb of 4:7-4:9 as its own row, but the lions illustrate rather than reopen the argument, and no fresh interrogative or vocative marks 4:10.
literature_type_guess: retribution proverb strophe: lion figure illustrating doom

boundary_rationale: “Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.” (web:Job.4.12; Hebrew וְ֭אֵלַי דָּבָ֣ר יְגֻנָּ֑ב) turns to Eliphaz's own night-vision testimony, a personal-voice register distinct from the preceding proverb. The strophe narrates the experience of the vision through its close, “It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,” (web:Job.4.16), whose final clause (דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע, ‘silence, then a voice I heard’) is a discourse frame introducing direct speech -- a perception clause with no verb of speaking, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family; the quoted content itself begins at 4:17, not before.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fold 4:17-4:21 into this row on the ground that the vision is one continuous unit through 4:21, but the shift from narrated experience to quoted oracle is itself marked by the discourse frame closing 4:16b -- a perception clause, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family -- and deserves its own row.
literature_type_guess: night-vision narrative: Eliphaz's oracle frame strophe

boundary_rationale: The quoted voice's oracle opens “Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?” (web:Job.4.17; Hebrew הַֽ֭אֱנוֹשׁ מֵאֱל֣וֹהַ יִצְדָּ֑ק, a byte-true interrogative-he construction -- the row's own near-edge driver, since 4:16's closing clause דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע (oshb:Job.4.16) carries no verb of speaking and belongs to no formula family; WEB's trailing 'saying,' bridges the two verses in translation only. The oracle runs to “Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.” (web:Job.4.21), which closes the embedded speech. Eliphaz's own voice resumes with a fresh imperative topic-turn at 5:1 (qra na), the seam bounding this row's far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carry the oracle through 5:1 as one continuous unit, since both open with rhetorical questions, but 5:1's qra na addresses Job directly in Eliphaz's own voice, not the vision's.
literature_type_guess: night-voice oracle: mortal frailty against divine judgment

boundary_rationale: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?” (web:Job.5.1; Hebrew קְֽרָא נָ֭א, ‘call now’) opens an imperative challenge paralleling the zkhor na of 4:7 (both topic-turn imperatives addressed to Job), and the strophe illustrates the fool's perishing down to “but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.” (web:Job.5.7), a proverbial close on man's trouble-bound birth. The following verse turns to Eliphaz's own stance with an adversative-plus-pronoun opening, marking the far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the fool's-fate illustration of 5:2-5:7 from the opening challenge of 5:1 as its own row, but the challenge and its illustration share one interrogative frame with no internal topic-turn.
literature_type_guess: fool's-fate strophe: uncontained wrath leads to ruin

boundary_rationale: “But as for me, I would seek God. I would commit my cause to God,” (web:Job.5.8; Hebrew אוּלָ֗ם אֲ֭נִי, ‘but as for me’) marks a stance shift: Eliphaz sets his own counsel (seeking God) against the fool just described, and the strophe catalogs divine providence through “So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.” (web:Job.5.16), which closes on the poor's hope and injustice's silenced mouth. The presentative hinneh reopens the address at 5:17, marking the far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Break this providence catalog at 5:12|5:13, where the crafty-versus-wise contrast sharpens, but no vocative, interrogative, or formula marks that internal point.
literature_type_guess: providence catalog: God's counsel against the fool's way

boundary_rationale: “Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.” (web:Job.5.17; Hebrew הִנֵּ֤ה אַשְׁרֵ֣י) opens the discipline-and-blessing strophe with the presentative hinneh, and the speech closes on a second presentative at “Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.” (web:Job.5.27; Hebrew הִנֵּה זֹ֭את), Eliphaz's own appeal to what he and his tradition have researched — verse-initial hinneh framing both edges of this row. The speech ends there: Job.6.1 opens “Then Job answered,” (web:Job.6.1) with the vaya'an formula under a new speaker token (Iyov); the formula closes Eliphaz's speech and opens Job's reply, corroborated (tier-3, single-witness) by the petuchah following oshb:Job.5.27.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Read the exhortation of 5:26-5:27 as a short coda separate from the discipline strophe of 5:17-5:25, but no interrogative, vocative, or formula opens 5:26, and both edges of the 5:17-5:27 span share the same hinneh framing.
literature_type_guess: discipline and blessing strophe: Eliphaz's closing hinneh frame

boundary_rationale: The seam at 5:27|6:1 is a speaker change: Eliphaz's admonition closes “Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.” web:Job.5.27, and the verse-initial formula וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.6.1) hands the floor to Job -- the tier-1 dialogue-formula spine's marker for a new voice, one of Job's eleven vaya'an-family tokens book-wide (sweep: 11 book-wide, per the formula inventory; Job also carries two vayosef-family tokens elsewhere in the dialogue, a distinct verb-family from vaya'an). Job opens by asking that his anguish be weighed, “Oh that my anguish were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!” web:Job.6.2, a weight he then declares “heavier than the sand of the seas” web:Job.6.3, names the Almighty's arrows and God's terrors as the cause of his rash words web:Job.6.4, then defends the outburst with a pair of settled-nature analogies, “Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder?” web:Job.6.5, extended by the tasteless-food pair web:Job.6.6, web:Job.6.7. The row keeps the formula and its immediate self-justification together as one opening movement of the reply.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Job.6.1 into its own row would isolate the bare formula from the self-justification it introduces, with no competing tier-1 signal before the wish-formula turn that follows.
literature_type_guess: Job's reply opens: affliction weight outweighs sand's measure

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative-wish opens the row: מִֽי יִ֭תֵּן תָּב֣וֹא שֶֽׁאֱלָתִ֑י וְ֝תִקְוָתִ֗י יִתֵּ֥ן אֱלֽוֹהַּ (oshb:Job.6.8), an instance of the dialogue-wide mi-yitten wish formula (sweep: 9 verses book-wide, 10 tokens, one verse carrying two, independently re-swept at skeleton tier). Job spells the wish out as a plea to be let go and cut off web:Job.6.9, holds his one consolation to be that he has “not denied the words of the Holy One” web:Job.6.10, then turns to a run of rhetorical questions about his exhausted capacity, “What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?” web:Job.6.11, “Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?” web:Job.6.12, closing on the admission that “wisdom is driven away from me” web:Job.6.13. The row ends before the next strophe's turn from Job's own exhausted capacity to a third-person accusation of the friends, opening at Job.6.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through Job.6.14 would merge the wish-formula lament with the brook-metaphor rebuke of the friends that follows it.
literature_type_guess: death wish strophe: Job seeks release from torment

boundary_rationale: A third-person topic shift opens the row: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.” web:Job.6.14 (Hebrew לַמָּ֣ס מֵרֵעֵ֣הוּ חָ֑סֶד וְיִרְאַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י יַעֲזֽוֹב, oshb:Job.6.14, grammatically third-person throughout -- the friend-word carries a 3ms suffix and the verb is 3ms imperfect, with no vocative particle), pivoting the subject-matter from Job's own exhaustion to a gnomic charge against companions in general. He extends the charge with the brook-caravan metaphor, “My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;” web:Job.6.15, traces the image through the melting ice and vanishing caravans of web:Job.6.16-Job.6.20, then the address itself turns second-person for the first time in the unit, “For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.” web:Job.6.21 (Hebrew כִּֽי עַ֭תָּה הֱיִ֣יתֶם לא ל֑וֹ תִּֽרְא֥וּ חֲ֝תַ֗ת וַתִּירָֽאוּ, oshb:Job.6.21, all second-person plural), before closing on a pair of denials that he ever asked the friends for a gift or ransom, web:Job.6.22-Job.6.23. This second-person address shift at 6:21 is a genuine tier-1 signal, not mere texture; it runs unbroken to the end of the chapter, and it is disclosed here as a live internal candidate for this unit's own seam rather than dismissed. It is not adopted as the row's own edge because the third-person charge and its direct application are held together as one movement of the friend-rebuke closing on Job's self-examination through 6:23; the alternative seam at 6:20|6:21 is disclosed here as a live, comparably warranted rival rather than resolved.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the row at Job.6.20|Job.6.21 for the second-person turn there is a live rival, not a texture-only consideration: 6:21 opens the unit's first 2mp forms and second-person address runs unbroken through 6:29 (nine verses, Job.6.21-Job.6.29), a comparably or better-warranted internal seam than the 6:23|6:24 edge kept here. It is disclosed rather than adopted because the row is held as one continuous rebuke of the friends across the third-person charge and its direct application; the question is left open rather than resolved, in the same spirit as the frame's own disclosed 2:6|2:7 crux.
literature_type_guess: friends rebuke: why abandon one brought low and helpless

boundary_rationale: An imperative shift opens the row: ה֭וֹרוּנִי וַאֲנִ֣י אַחֲרִ֑ישׁ וּמַה שָּׁ֝גִ֗יתִי הָבִ֥ינוּ לִֽי (oshb:Job.6.24), Job's invitation to be corrected rather than the denial he had just voiced. He weighs “words of uprightness” against the friends' empty reproof web:Job.6.25, protests that their reproof treats the speeches of one who is desperate as mere wind while they would gamble away the fatherless web:Job.6.26-Job.6.27, then appeals directly, “Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.” web:Job.6.28, repeats the appeal, “Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.” web:Job.6.29, and closes on a self-examining question, “Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?” web:Job.6.30. The row runs from the imperative petition to the end of the chapter, closing Job's rebuke of the friends before the reply turns, in the next chapter, to a meditation on human toil in general.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the row back to include the brook-metaphor rebuke above it would stretch one strophe well past a comfortable length without an intervening tier-1 seam to justify the span. A second rival was weighed at this row's own near edge: 6:28 opens with the ve'attah turn, וְ֭עַתָּה הוֹאִ֣ילוּ פְנוּ בִ֑י וְעַל פְּ֝נֵיכֶ֗ם אִם אֲכַזֵּֽב (oshb:Job.6.28) -- a device that sweeps 8 book-wide (Job.6.28, Job.30.1, Job.30.9, Job.30.16, Job.35.15, Job.37.21, Job.42.5, Job.42.8) and keys strophe structure elsewhere in the book -- followed at 6:29 by an imperative-plus-na, שֻֽׁבוּ נָ֭א אַל תְּהִ֣י עַוְלָ֑ה ושבי וְשׁ֥וּבוּ ע֝וֹד צִדְקִי בָֽהּ (oshb:Job.6.29), the same form-class opening 5:1 (קְֽרָא נָ֭א) and 4:7 (זְכָר נָ֗א). Splitting at 6:27|6:28 was rejected because 6:28's appeal ('look at me... I will not lie to your face') and 6:29's renewed imperative ('return... my cause is righteous') both continue rather than reopen the direct appeal Job begins at 6:24 -- one imperative-headed appeal running from ה֭וֹרוּנִי at 6:24 through the self-examining close at 6:30 -- so the row is kept whole through both internal signals rather than split at either.
literature_type_guess: Job appeals: teach me what error caused this punishment

boundary_rationale: The speech turns from direct address of the friends to a general reflection on human toil, opening with a rhetorical question about shared hardship rather than a second-person accusation: “Isn’t a man forced to labor on earth? Aren’t his days like the days of a hired hand?” web:Job.7.1. Job compares himself to “a servant who earnestly desires the shadow” web:Job.7.2, applies the image to his own “months of misery” and wearisome nights web:Job.7.3, describes lying awake until dawn web:Job.7.4, and catalogs his bodily affliction, “My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust. My skin closes up, and breaks out afresh.” web:Job.7.5, closing on “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.” web:Job.7.6. The row ends before the imperative that turns the complaint toward God directly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading Job.7.1 as a continuation of chapter six's direct rebuke would erase the shift from second-person accusation to a general reflection on human labor.
literature_type_guess: hardship complaint strophe: hired servant and restless nights

boundary_rationale: An imperative addressed to God opens the row: זְ֭כֹר כִּי ר֣וּחַ חַיָּ֑י לֹא תָשׁ֥וּב עֵ֝ינִ֗י לִרְא֥וֹת טֽוֹב (oshb:Job.7.7), “Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye will no more see good.” web:Job.7.7. The row stays with mortality across four verses: the eye that will see him no more web:Job.7.8, the cloud that vanishes and the one who goes down to Sheol web:Job.7.9, and the house and place that will no longer know him web:Job.7.10. The unit is short, but it is bounded on both sides by a change of mode -- the imperative petition opening it and the self-assertive resolve of the next strophe closing it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Job.7.7-10 as a continuation of the toil meditation above it would erase the imperative address-shift that opens it and turns the complaint to address God directly rather than the human audience.
literature_type_guess: remembrance complaint: God will not relent or acknowledge

boundary_rationale: An emphatic self-reference opens a new resolve: גַּם אֲנִי֮ לֹ֤א אֶחֱשָׂ֫ךְ פִּ֥י אֲֽ֭דַבְּרָה בְּצַ֣ר רוּחִ֑י אָ֝שִׂ֗יחָה בְּמַ֣ר נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Job.7.11), “Therefore I will not keep silent. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.” web:Job.7.11. Job asks “Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?” web:Job.7.12, describes a bed that fails to comfort him because God frightens him with dreams web:Job.7.13-Job.7.14, and concludes that his soul “chooses strangling, death rather than my bones” web:Job.7.15, then states outright, “I loathe my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.” web:Job.7.16. The row runs from the fronted-pronoun resolve to the loathing-of-life statement it produces, ending before the next topic-turn interrogative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at Job.7.10 would cut the fronted-pronoun resolve of Job.7.11 away from the dream-terror and life-loathing material it introduces.
literature_type_guess: mortality complaint: days flee like fleeting wind patterns

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the row's final movement: מָֽה אֱ֭נוֹשׁ כִּ֣י תְגַדְּלֶ֑נּוּ וְכִי תָשִׁ֖ית אֵלָ֣יו לִבֶּֽךָ (oshb:Job.7.17), “What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him,” web:Job.7.17, continuing the direct address to God with the daily scrutiny of web:Job.7.18, the plea “How long will you not look away from me” web:Job.7.19, and the accusation of being made a “mark” and a “burden” web:Job.7.20 -- a verse that itself carries a paseq segment, tier-3 and single-witness -- closing the speech on “Why do you not pardon my disobedience, and take away my iniquity? For now will I lie down in the dust. You will seek me diligently, but I will not be.” web:Job.7.21. That closing verse also carries a petuchah notation and a paseq segment, both single-witness and both tier-3 at most, corroborating rather than driving the close of the reply here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging Job.7.17-21 into the row above it would run the Job.7.11 resolve's aftermath and the closing interrogative movement together past a comfortable strophe length.
literature_type_guess: divine arbitration impossibility: no umpire between Job and God

boundary_rationale: The verse-initial formula וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשּׁוּחִ֗י וַיֹאמַֽר (oshb:Job.8.1) hands the speech to Bildad; the WEB rendering is “Then Bildad the Shuhite answered,” web:Job.8.1. Bildad's vaya'an-formula family sums to three speeches book-wide across two gentilic spellings, named per member: the plene הַשּׁוּחִ֗י opening this verse (byte tier; the plene spelling itself sweeps 3 book-wide at 2:11, 8:1, 42:9, but only 8:1 is a formula opening), and the defective הַשֻּׁחִ֗י opening his later two speeches, oshb:Job.18.1 and oshb:Job.25.1 (byte tier; sweeps 2 book-wide). The family total of three formula members is a sum across these two named spellings, not one blended string. Bildad rebukes Job's outburst, “How long will you speak these things? Shall the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?” web:Job.8.2, states his retribution doctrine as a rhetorical denial, “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?” web:Job.8.3, applies it to Job's dead children web:Job.8.4, and offers the conditional promise that follows from the doctrine, “If you want to seek God diligently, make your supplication to the Almighty.” web:Job.8.5, “If you were pure and upright, surely now he would awaken for you, and make the habitation of your righteousness prosperous.” web:Job.8.6, closing on the promise that “your latter end would greatly increase” web:Job.8.7. The row runs from the speech formula through the doctrine's opening statement, ending before Bildad turns to an appeal to ancestral precedent.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating Job.8.1 as its own row would separate Bildad's formula from the doctrine it introduces without a competing tier-1 signal before the imperative appeal to precedent that follows.
literature_type_guess: Bildad opens: ancient wisdom on retribution doctrine

boundary_rationale: An imperative pivots Bildad's argument from assertion to appeal: כִּֽי שְׁאַל נָ֭א לְדֹ֣ר רִישׁ֑וֹן וְ֝כוֹנֵ֗ן לְחֵ֣קֶר אֲבוֹתָֽם (oshb:Job.8.8), “Please inquire of past generations. Find out about the learning of their fathers.” web:Job.8.8. He grounds the appeal in his own generation's limits, “For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days on earth are a shadow.” web:Job.8.9, and closes the appeal with a rhetorical question about what the ancestors would teach, web:Job.8.10. The row is short, but it sits between two tier-1 signals rather than resting on verse count alone: the imperative that opens it and the topic-turn interrogative about the papyrus that opens the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this appeal into the doctrine row above it would erase the imperative shift from assertion to appeal-to-precedent that begins it.
literature_type_guess: ancestral wisdom claim: former fathers knew this truth

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the nature parable: הֲיִֽגְאֶה גֹּ֭מֶא בְּלֹ֣א בִצָּ֑ה יִשְׂגֶּה אָ֥חוּ בְלִי מָֽיִם (oshb:Job.8.11), “Can the papyrus grow up without mire? Can the rushes grow without water?” web:Job.8.11. Bildad extends the plant image through its premature withering web:Job.8.12, applies it to “all who forget God” whose hope is a “spider's web” web:Job.8.13-Job.8.14, describes a house that will not stand web:Job.8.15, and elaborates a second plant image of roots wrapped around a rock pile web:Job.8.16-Job.8.17, ending on the plant's erasure from its place and the ironic close, “Behold, this is the joy of his way. Out of the earth, others will spring.” web:Job.8.18-Job.8.19. The presentative הן also opens Job.8.20 immediately after (הֶן אֵ֭ל לֹ֣א יִמְאַס תָּ֑ם וְלֹֽא יַ֝חֲזִ֗יק בְּיַד מְרֵעִֽים, oshb:Job.8.20) -- but 8:20 is third person throughout, its two finite verbs both 3ms with no second-person morpheme. The shift this row's edge actually rests on is the grammatical subject, not the addressee: 8:11-8:19 traces the fate of 'him who forgets God' in the third person through a plant figure, and 8:20 closes that figure with a hen-headed maxim whose subject becomes God himself (still third person) -- a different pivot from the direct second-person promise that follows one verse later, at 8:21 (inside the next row). One further nuance on this row's own near edge: 8:18 itself closes on לֹ֣א רְאִיתִֽיךָ, a second-person suffix, but it sits inside the plant-figure's own quoted denial rather than the narrator's direct address to Job, so the third-person/second-person contrast this row's edges draw is not perfectly morphological on either side, and is disclosed as such.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through Job.8.20-22 would run the third-person plant parable together with the hen-headed maxim's subject-shift to God at 8:20 and the direct second-person promise that follows it at 8:21, erasing a genuine grammatical turn even though that turn is a subject shift rather than an address shift at its own opening verse.
literature_type_guess: hypocrite destruction: papyrus withers and web collapses

boundary_rationale: The presentative הן reopens the row with the hen-headed maxim that closes the plant parable's argument, still third person throughout: הֶן אֵ֭ל לֹ֣א יִמְאַס תָּ֑ם וְלֹֽא יַ֝חֲזִ֗יק בְּיַד מְרֵעִֽים (oshb:Job.8.20), “Behold, God will not cast away a blameless man, neither will he uphold the evildoers.” web:Job.8.20 -- its subject is God, not yet Job by address. The direct second-person promise to Job begins one verse later, inside this same row: “He will still fill your mouth with laughter, your lips with shouting.” web:Job.8.21 (Hebrew פִּ֑יךָ וּשְׂפָתֶ֥יךָ, both 2ms-suffixed, oshb:Job.8.21), and closes the speech, “Those who hate you will be clothed with shame. The tent of the wicked will be no more.” web:Job.8.22, which also carries a petuchah notation, single-witness and tier-3, corroborating the close. The seam at 8:22|9:1 is a return of the dialogue-formula spine: וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.9.1), “Then Job answered,” web:Job.9.1, repeats byte-for-byte the same formula that opened Job's reply at web:Job.6.1, the start of this part, handing the floor back to Job and closing Bildad's speech at Job.8.22.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Job.8.20-22 back into the nature-parable row would run the hen-headed maxim's subject-shift to God at 8:20, and the direct second-person promise that follows it at 8:21, together with the third-person description of the godless man's collapse that precedes 8:20.
literature_type_guess: hope renewed: God will fill thy mouth with laughter

boundary_rationale: The vaya'an formula וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (Job.9.1) opens a fresh speech-turn immediately after Bildad's unrenewed close at web:Job.8.22 (“Those who hate you will be clothed with shame” web:Job.8.22), matching the tier-1 speaker-change spine that governs every dialogue seam in the book. Job's programmatic question “how can man be just with God” web:Job.9.2 sets the thesis that Job.9.3-Job.9.4 immediately supports: no one can answer God “one time in a thousand” web:Job.9.3, and none who hardened himself against him has prospered (web:Job.9.4), a thesis-plus-support pair that closes before the participial hymn opens at Job.9.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the strophe at Job.9.2 alone was rejected because the wisdom-and-strength question of Job.9.4 completes the thesis rather than opening a new one.
literature_type_guess: Job's reply to Bildad: God's wisdom and might acknowledged

boundary_rationale: A chain of article-plus-participle predications about God opens this strophe: הַמַּעְתִּ֣יק (glossed ‘the one who removes’, Job.9.5), הַמַּרְגִּ֣יז (glossed ‘the one who shakes’, Job.9.6), and הָאֹמֵ֣ר (glossed ‘the one who commands’, Job.9.7) describe cosmic acts ( “He removes the mountains, and they don't know it” web:Job.9.5 ), continuing through the anarthrous participle עֹשֶׂ֣ה that closes the catalogue at Job.9.10 ( “He does great things past finding out; yes, marvelous things without number.” web:Job.9.10 ). Job.9.11 opens הֵ֤ן יַעֲבֹ֣ר עָ֭לַי (glossed ‘behold, he passes by me’) and Job.9.12 opens הֵ֣ן יַ֭חְתֹּף (glossed ‘behold, he snatches away’): a twin presentative opening (הֵ֤ן/הֵ֣ן), not a further participle, moving the same unopposable power from cosmos to Job's own experience ( “Who will ask him, 'What are you doing?'” web:Job.9.12 ), and the strophe closes on the mythic image שָׁ֝חֲח֗וּ עֹ֣זְרֵי רָֽהַב (glossed ‘Rahab's helpers stoop’, Job.9.13), summarizing the whole unit before the a-fortiori pivot of Job.9.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Job.9.11-Job.9.12 into their own strophe at Job.9.10|Job.9.11 is a genuine rival: the article/anarthrous-participle catalogue predicating God actually ends at Job.9.10, and Job.9.11-Job.9.12 open with a twin presentative plus finite verbs — הֵ֤ן יַעֲבֹ֣ר עָ֭לַי (Job.9.11) and הֵ֣ן יַ֭חְתֹּף (Job.9.12) — not a further participle; this presentative-opening class (הֵ֤ן/הֵ֣ן) is a tier-1 topic-turn signal elsewhere in the book (sweep: 30 verse-initial tokens of this presentative book-wide, skeleton tier, with only 3 adjacent-verse pairs, this one among them). This row keeps Job.9.5-Job.9.13 unified anyway because no address, addressee, or discourse-frame change accompanies the participle-to-finite-verb shift: the same unopposable-power argument Job opens at Job.9.4 (“God is wise in heart, and mighty in strength. Who has hardened himself against him and prospered?” web:Job.9.4) is read here as running, without interruption, from that opening through the twin-presentative application to Job's own case and on to the Rahab image that closes Job.9.13 -- a continuity claim that itself crosses this row's own near seam at Job.9.4|Job.9.5, disclosed here as a straddle rather than resolved; the rival seam at Job.9.10|Job.9.11 is real but this row treats the grammatical-mood shift as intensification of one argument rather than a fresh topic.
literature_type_guess: divine power hymn: cosmic orders and earthquake shaking

boundary_rationale: An a-fortiori particle opens the strophe: אַ֭ף כִּֽי (glossed ‘how much less’, Job.9.14), drawing the direct implication from the preceding power-hymn that Job himself cannot answer God. A chain of אם-protases follows (Job.9.15-Job.9.16, Job.9.19-Job.9.20) arguing that no hearing could be fair even for an innocent man: “Though I am righteous, my own mouth will condemn me” web:Job.9.20. The strophe closes on the bare declarative תָּֽם אָ֭נִי (“I am blameless. I don't respect myself. I despise my life.” web:Job.9.21), a personal verdict that ends the courtroom-inability argument before the inferential turn of Job.9.22.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing this strophe at Job.9.20 was rejected because Job.9.21's self-verdict completes the courtroom argument's clause chain rather than opening an unrelated one.
literature_type_guess: complaint of innocence: all alike perish by divine hand

boundary_rationale: An explicit quotative frame opens this short strophe: אַחַ֗ת הִ֥יא עַל כֵּ֥ן (glossed ‘it is all one; therefore I say’, Job.9.22), introducing the indictment “he destroys the blameless and the wicked” web:Job.9.22. This opening word, תָּ֥ם (‘blameless’), repeats — at byte tier — the word that twice closes the preceding strophe's argument (תָּֽם at Job.9.20 word 5, תָּֽם at Job.9.21 word 1), a cross-seam lexical bond disclosed here rather than left implicit; it corroborates continuity of the courtroom-to-indictment argument across 9.21|9.22 without moving either strophe's edge. Job.9.23-Job.9.24 extend the same indictment: Job.9.22's מְכַלֶּֽה (‘destroys’) carries an explicit third-person subject, ה֣וּא, and Job.9.23's נְקִיִּ֣ם (‘mocks’) has no expressed subject of its own — WEB's own rendering keeps the pronoun 'he' across the verse boundary rather than naming 'the scourge' as a fresh subject, so the mocking agent is left as open a question in the Hebrew as in English; either way the indictment stays continuous, reaching “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked” web:Job.9.24, closing on the rhetorical question “If not he, then who is it?” web:Job.9.24. The subject shifts from this cosmic indictment to Job's own fleeting days at Job.9.25, marking the strophe's far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Job.9.22-Job.9.24 into the preceding courtroom-inability argument was rejected given the explicit inferential frame that opens Job.9.22 and the fresh third-person subject (earth, judges) it introduces.
literature_type_guess: theodicy indictment: God mocks the calamity of innocent

boundary_rationale: The fronted possessive subject וְיָמַ֣י קַ֭לּוּ (“Now my days are swifter than a runner” web:Job.9.25) turns the topic from the theodicy indictment to Job's own vanishing lifespan, using simile (“as the swift ships, as the eagle that swoops on the prey” web:Job.9.26). A pair of אם-protases then brackets the futility of self-vindication: Job.9.27 ( “I will forget my complaint” web:Job.9.27 ) and Job.9.30 ( washing with snow ), both resolving to the same fear ( “I know that you will not hold me innocent” web:Job.9.28 ) and closing on “My own clothes will abhor me” web:Job.9.31, before the כי-clause of Job.9.32 reopens the courtroom register directly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A break at Job.9.27|Job.9.28 was considered but rejected since the paired אם-protases of Job.9.27 and Job.9.30 frame one continuous argument about the futility of self-cleansing.
literature_type_guess: fleeting days complaint: life flies like courier and shuttle

boundary_rationale: A כי-clause reopens the courtroom register at the strophe's entry: כִּי לֹא אִ֣ישׁ כָּמֹ֣נִי (“For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him” web:Job.9.32), leading to the complaint “There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both” web:Job.9.33 and the wish that follows: “Let him take his rod away from me” web:Job.9.34, closing on Job's claim to a fearless voice if the terror were lifted ( “I would speak, and not fear him” web:Job.9.35 ). No vaya'an or vayosef intervenes before Job.10.1, so the reply continues; the strophe division tracks the chapter edge because a fresh self-report in Job's own voice opens Job.10.1 rather than the courtroom wish continuing.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through Job.10.1 remains rejected, but not because the two verses are lexically disconnected: אַֽ֭דַבְּרָה, the word that opens this strophe's own closing wish at Job.9.35, recurs, skeleton-identical, as the word that closes Job.10.1 (אֲ֝דַבְּרָה֗) — word-exact skeleton sweep: 6 book-wide (Job.7.11, Job.9.35, Job.10.1, Job.16.4, Job.16.6, Job.32.20), and Job.9.35|Job.10.1 is the only book-order-adjacent pair; a further match at Job.13.13 is prefixed (מִ֭מֶּנִּי), substring-level only. Job.10.1 also reuses, byte-identical, שִׂיחִ֑י from Job.9.27 (sweep: 3 book-wide, with Job.21.4) and, skeleton-identical, אֶעֶזְבָ֖ה from the same verse (sweep: 2 book-wide) — real catchwords straddling this row's own far seam, disclosed here rather than denied. The boundary is kept anyway because Job.10.1 opens with its own fresh 1cs discourse-frame verb, נָֽקְטָ֥ה ('my soul is weary'), a new formal restart rather than a continuation of the prior clause; the shared vocabulary reads as a deliberate reprise bridging two strophes of one unbroken speech, not as evidence the seam itself is misplaced.
literature_type_guess: divine umpire plea: no arbiter exists between us both

boundary_rationale: A fresh self-report opens the strophe: נָֽקְטָ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֗י (“My soul is weary of my life” web:Job.10.1), followed by the discourse frame אֹמַ֣ר אֶל אֱ֭לוֹהַּ (“I will tell God, 'Do not condemn me” web:Job.10.2), introducing direct second-person address to the deity that governs the rest of the strophe. Job.10.3-Job.10.7 carry that same address entirely through pronominal suffixes and verb morphology rather than any independent second-person pronoun — the 2ms independent pronoun sweeps 10 times book-wide and occurs nowhere in chapter 10 — with the interrogative particle heading three of the seven verses: “Do you have eyes of flesh? Or do you see as man sees?” web:Job.10.4, “Are your days as the days of mortals” web:Job.10.5. Job.10.6 continues the same question under כִּֽי rather than a fresh interrogative, and Job.10.7 turns concessive, “Although you know that I am not wicked” web:Job.10.7 (WEB's own rendering), closing on “there is no one who can deliver out of your hand” web:Job.10.7 before the address turns to God's creative handiwork at Job.10.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Stopping the strophe at Job.10.6 was rejected because Job.10.7 continues the same second-person complaint under a concessive clause (“Although you know that I am not wicked” web:Job.10.7) before the address shifts to the creation imagery opening Job.10.8, even though the interrogative particle itself does not extend past Job.10.5.
literature_type_guess: complaint and accusation: why hide face and treat as foe

boundary_rationale: The strophe turns from the oppression-themed interrogatives to creation imagery with a fronted address: יָדֶ֣יךָ עִ֭צְּבוּנִי, “Your hands have framed me and fashioned me altogether, yet you destroy me.” web:Job.10.8 — the same verse that opens the strophe on gift-language closes on the identical undoing threatened at the strophe's far edge. Job.10.9 asks “Will you bring me into dust again?” web:Job.10.9, a second reminder that the creation imagery already carries its own destruction inside this strophe, not just across the seam at Job.10.13. The imagery continues through the positive acts of formation, “clothed me with skin and flesh” web:Job.10.11, and closes on “Your visitation has preserved my spirit” web:Job.10.12, before the adversative pivot of Job.10.13 makes explicit, through a fronted demonstrative object not used earlier in the strophe, the hostility that Job.10.8-Job.10.9 have already voiced twice in passing.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging Job.10.8-Job.10.12 with the accusation that follows was rejected because the adversative fronting at Job.10.13 — not merely destructive content, which already appears in passing at Job.10.8-Job.10.9 — marks the genuine hinge into direct, sustained accusation.
literature_type_guess: creation imagery strophe: hands formed and womb's nourishment

boundary_rationale: An adversative waw fronts the demonstrative object at the strophe's entry: וְ֭אֵלֶּה צָפַ֣נְתָּ בִלְבָבֶ֑ךָ (“Yet you hid these things in your heart” web:Job.10.13), pivoting from the preceding creation-gift imagery to an accusation of concealed hostile intent that runs through Job.10.17: “You renew your witnesses against me, and increase your indignation on me” web:Job.10.17. The strophe's close on “Changes and warfare are with me” web:Job.10.17 gives way to the birth-and-death lament that opens Job.10.18.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this strophe through Job.10.18 was rejected since the birth-lament question of Job.10.18 opens a distinct death-wish unit rather than continuing the renewed-witnesses accusation.
literature_type_guess: concealed hostility accusation: why reveal and then hide

boundary_rationale: A fresh rhetorical question opens the closing strophe of Job's reply: וְלָ֣מָּה מֵ֭רֶחֶם הֹצֵאתָ֑נִי (“Why, then, have you brought me out of the womb?” web:Job.10.18), turning from the renewed-hostility accusation to a death-wish that runs to the chapter's end: “I should have been as though I had not been” web:Job.10.19, “Leave me alone, that I may find a little comfort” web:Job.10.20, closing on the land of darkness, “where the light is as midnight” web:Job.10.22. A petuchah follows Job.10.22 (oshb:Job.10.22 (petuchah, single-witness)), single-witness tier-3 corroboration, consistent with the strophe's close before Zophar's formula opens Job.11.1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Job.10.18-Job.10.22 as a continuation of the prior accusation was rejected not because the verse opens without a particle — it opens with a vav-fronted construction, like this speech's other strophe-initial pivot at Job.10.13 (וְ֭אֵלֶּה, an adversative waw fronting a demonstrative object) — but here the vav fronts an interrogative instead (וְלָ֣מָּה, 'why') — but because the verse introduces a fresh rhetorical question on an unrelated topic (why brought from the womb, a birth/death lament) rather than continuing the surveillance-and-hostility accusation of Job.10.13-Job.10.17; the topic shift, not the shared vav-initial shape, is what forms the unbroken death-wish unit running through the chapter's end.
literature_type_guess: death's preference: return to womb before the grave

boundary_rationale: Zophar's own vaya'an formula, וַ֭יַּעַן צֹפַ֥ר הַֽנַּעֲמָתִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר (Job.11.1), opens a new speech-turn, the clearest tier-1 signal available, immediately following Job's own close at Job.10.22 (petuchah, single-witness). His rebuke opens with הֲרֹ֣ב דְּ֭בָרִים לֹ֣א יֵעָנֶ֑ה (glossed ‘shouldn't the multitude of words be answered?’, Job.11.2) and continues in direct second-person address through וַ֭תֹּאמֶר זַ֣ךְ לִקְחִ֑י (“For you say, 'My doctrine is pure” web:Job.11.4). The wish מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן אֱל֣וֹהַּ דַּבֵּ֑ר (“oh that God would speak” web:Job.11.5) continues the same second-person address into Job.11.6; this wish-clause pattern (skeleton-tier מי יתן sweep: 9 verses / 10 tokens book-wide) elsewhere carries Job's own voice, but here belongs to Zophar, and any reading of the formula as Job-exclusive must disclose this member. The strophe closes on “God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves” web:Job.11.6 before the theological register shifts at Job.11.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Excluding Job.11.5-Job.11.6 from this opening strophe was rejected since the wish clause continues the same second-person rebuke begun at Job.11.2 without any intervening formula.
literature_type_guess: Zophar opens: importunate speech and shallow wisdom rebuke

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens still in second-person address — הַחֵ֣קֶר אֱל֣וֹהַ תִּמְצָ֑א אִ֤ם עַד תַּכְלִ֖ית שַׁדַּ֣י תִּמְצָֽא (“Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty?” web:Job.11.7) and its parallel, גָּבְהֵ֣י שָׁ֭מַיִם מַה תִּפְעָ֑ל עֲמֻקָּ֥ה מִ֝שְּׁא֗וֹל מַה תֵּדָֽע (“...What can you do?...What can you know?” web:Job.11.8), carry four 2ms verbs between them (תִּמְצָ֑א and תִּמְצָֽא -- skeleton-tier match, distinct pointed forms; תִּפְעָ֑ל, תֵּדָֽע), continuing rather than breaking the second-person rebuke that opens this speech. The turn to third-person description is not the topic-turn interrogative itself but comes one verse later: Job.11.9's nominal clause (no expressed addressee) and, unambiguously, the 3ms protasis of Job.11.10 (אִם יַחֲלֹ֥ף וְיַסְגִּ֑יר, glossed 'if he passes by, or confines') running through Job.11.11's explicit third-person subject, כִּי ה֭וּא יָדַ֣ע מְתֵי שָׁ֑וְא (“For he knows false men” web:Job.11.11). The strophe closes on the proverb וְעַ֥יִר פֶּ֝֗רֶא אָדָ֥ם יִוָּלֵֽד (“a man is born as a wild donkey's colt” web:Job.11.12), before the address returns to second person at Job.11.13. The strophe boundary itself still rests on the topic-turn interrogative opening Job.11.7 (unsearchable-depths questions distinct from Job.11.2-Job.11.6's direct rebuke), not on a person shift that in fact arrives two verses later.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating Job.11.7-Job.11.8's second-person questions from Job.11.9-Job.11.12's third-person description was considered but rejected because both halves elaborate one shared claim about God's inescapable, unsearchable knowledge before the address shifts back to Job at Job.11.13.
literature_type_guess: divine inscrutability: God's judgment deeper than earth's foundation

boundary_rationale: The address returns to second person at the strophe's entry, אִם אַ֭תָּ֗ה (glossed ‘if you’, Job.11.13): “If you set your heart aright, stretch out your hands toward him” web:Job.11.13. A protasis-apodosis block follows, resolving at Job.11.15 with כִּי אָ֤ז (glossed ‘surely then’): “Surely then you will lift up your face without spot” web:Job.11.15, and the promise chain continues unbroken through Job.11.19 ( “many will court your favor” web:Job.11.19 ). The closing antithesis, וְעֵינֵ֥י רְשָׁעִ֗ים (“But the eyes of the wicked will fail” web:Job.11.20), ends Zophar's speech; a petuchah follows (oshb:Job.11.20 (petuchah, single-witness)), tier-3 corroboration. Zophar's speech closes here: Job's own vaya'an formula reopens immediately at Job.12.1, the same tier-1 speaker-change spine that opened Job.9.1, marking the seam between the two speeches.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this strophe at Job.11.15 was rejected because the promise clauses of Job.11.16-Job.11.19 continue the same apodosis chain that Job.11.15 opens, before the antithesis of Job.11.20 closes it.
literature_type_guess: turn and seek strophe: repentance leads to restoration

boundary_rationale: The formula וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר “Then Job answered,” web:Job.12.1 opens this row and the whole row-set: it is one of the book's eleven vaya'an tokens attributed to Job's own speaker-token (plus two vayosef tokens elsewhere, thirteen Job-attributed verse-initial formulas total, per the book's speech-formula inventory), and it immediately follows Zophar's closing gnomic warning about the wicked's “giving up of the spirit” web:Job.11.20 - a speaker change (Zophar to Job) that is the strongest available tier-1 seam. A petuchah follows 11:20 in the Masoretic tradition (oshb:Job.11.20 (petuchah, single-witness)), corroborating without driving the formula-marked opening of this speech. Job answers with direct second-person-plural address to the friends: אַתֶּם עָ֑ם “you are the people” web:Job.12.2, then לֹא נֹפֵ֣ל אָנֹכִ֣י מִכֶּ֑ם “I am not inferior to you” web:Job.12.3 (this exact four-word clause recurs, consonant-for-consonant, at 13:2 (skeleton-tier sweep: 2 book-wide; byte tier is 1 — נֹפֵ֣ל carries munach and מִכֶּ֑ם carries etnachta here, while נֹפֵ֖ל carries tipcha and מִכֶּֽם carries meteg at 13:2 — a consonantal, not byte-identical, repetition) - closing an inclusio completed at Job.13.2). At 12:4 the address drops away and Job turns to report his own case: שְׂחֹ֤ק לְרֵעֵ֨הוּ אֶֽהְיֶ֗ה “I am like one who is a joke to his neighbor” web:Job.12.4, a fronted-predicate register shift from arguing with the friends to describing his own humiliation. The strophe closes on the wicked's ease: וּֽ֭בַטֻּחוֹת לְמַרְגִּ֣יזֵי אֵ֑ל לַאֲשֶׁ֤ר הֵבִ֖יא אֱל֣וֹהַּ בְּיָדֽוֹ “Those who provoke God are secure, who carry their god in their hands” web:Job.12.6, pairing the bare divine name El with Eloah in the same line (Eloah belongs to the book's divine-name distribution, sweep: 37 tokens book-wide, confined to poetry chapters and absent from the prose frame) before the imperative that opens the next strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Starting the row at 12:2 and letting 12:1's formula stand as a bare one-word seam marker on its own was rejected, since a one-clause narrative tag carries no strophe content by itself.
literature_type_guess: Job's third response: friends address and wisdom mockery

boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative opens the row: וְֽאוּלָ֗ם שְׁאַל נָ֣א בְהֵמ֣וֹת וְתֹרֶ֑ךָּ “But ask the animals now, and they will teach you” web:Job.12.7. The word rendered “animals” here is the common plural of behemah (word-exact skeleton sweep: 2 book-wide, independently re-derived: 12:7 and 40:15 only), and it is a distinct homograph from the named creature at 40:15 - a general “ask the beasts” idiom here, kept separate from the later creature's count rather than blended with it. The catalog of witnesses (animals, birds, earth, fish) climaxes in the row's most disputed line: כִּ֥י יַד יְ֝הוָה עָ֣שְׂתָה זֹּֽאת “Yahweh's hand has done this” web:Job.12.9, the bare Tetragrammaton (sweep: 29 tokens / 22 verses book-wide, independently re-derived by exact word-skeleton match) appearing here as its sole occurrence inside the human dialogue - every other bare token sits in the prose frame (ch.1-2, 12 verses), the epilogue (42:7-17, 4 of its verses), or one of five remaining formula-adjacent verses in ch.38/40/42: the two storm-phrase formulas that reopen YHWH's own speeches (Job.38.1's qere מִ֥ן הַסְּעָרָ֗ה, ketiv מנ הסערה, single-witness; Job.40.6's qere מִ֥ן סְעָרָ֗ה, ketiv מנ סערה, single-witness), YHWH's second speech-opening at Job.40.1 (וַיַּ֖עַן יְהוָ֥ה אֶת אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר), and the two verses where Job's own vaya'an formula names YHWH as its object (אֶת יְהוָ֗ה) instead of opening a YHWH speech -- Job.40.3, the second of ch.40's three bare tokens, and Job.42.1 -- both reading וַיַּ֖עַן אִיּ֥וֹב אֶת יְהוָ֗ה וַיֹּאמַֽר, not a YHWH speech at all. The row continues past this anomaly without a fresh formula, vocative, or address shift: אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ֭יָדוֹ נֶ֣פֶשׁ כָּל חָ֑י “in whose hand is the life of every living thing” web:Job.12.10 is a relative clause continuing v.9's thought, and הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן “Doesn't the ear try words” web:Job.12.11 pivots to a proverb on discernment, closing with בִּֽישִׁישִׁ֥ים חָכְמָ֑ה “With aged men is wisdom” web:Job.12.12 - answered directly by the next row's opening claim that wisdom belongs to God, not merely to age.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carving 12:9 into its own one-verse row around the anomalous bare Yahweh token was rejected, since no formula, vocative, or discourse-frame turn isolates it from the surrounding creation-testimony catalog.
literature_type_guess: animal instruction strophe: beasts and birds teach wisdom

boundary_rationale: עִ֭מּוֹ חָכְמָ֣ה וּגְבוּרָ֑ה “With God is wisdom and might” web:Job.12.13 answers the preceding proverb's claim that wisdom lies with the aged (12:12) by relocating it in God outright - a clear topic-turn from human epistemology to divine attribute. A behold-pair follows: הֵ֣ן יַ֭הֲרוֹס וְלֹ֣א יִבָּנֶ֑ה “he breaks down, and it can't be built again” web:Job.12.14, and הֵ֤ן יַעְצֹ֣ר בַּמַּ֣יִם וְיִבָ֑שׁוּ “he withholds the waters, and they dry up” web:Job.12.15. The strophe closes by repeating its own opening word: עִ֭מּוֹ עֹ֣ז וְתֽוּשִׁיָּ֑ה “With him is strength and wisdom” web:Job.12.16, an exact verse-initial refrain (sweep: 2 book-wide, exclusively at 12:13 and 12:16, independently re-derived) that brackets this thesis quatrain before the next row unpacks it into named reversals.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this row through 12:25 to keep the whole hymn as one span was set aside because the verse-initial refrain at 12:16 closes a self-contained thesis before the concrete catalog of reversals begins.
literature_type_guess: divine wisdom hymn: strength and counsel with God eternally

boundary_rationale: Once the inclusio bracketing Job.12.13-Job.12.16 closes on its own repeated opener (עִ֭מּוֹ, sweep: 3 book-wide; its companion pronoun ל֝֗וֹ, sweep: 4 book-wide; the two co-occur in exactly 2 verses book-wide, both at 12:13/12:16), the row opens a concrete list with no new formula or particle of its own: מוֹלִ֣יךְ יוֹעֲצִ֣ים שׁוֹלָ֑ל וְֽשֹׁפְטִ֥ים יְהוֹלֵֽל, “He leads counselors away stripped. He makes judges fools.” web:Job.12.17, continuing through kings (12:18), priests and the mighty (12:19), elders (12:20), and princes (12:21) before broadening to nations and their leaders: רָאשֵׁ֣י עַם הָאָ֑רֶץ “the chiefs of the people of the earth” web:Job.12.24. The catalog ends on a disorientation image, יְמַֽשְׁשׁוּ חֹ֥שֶׁךְ וְלֹא א֑וֹר וַ֝יַּתְעֵ֗ם כַּשִּׁכּֽוֹר “They grope in the dark without light. He makes them stagger like a drunken man.” web:Job.12.25, closing chapter 12; content, not the chapter number, drives the edge here - the wicked's would-be wisdom collapses into the same darkness the hymn opened by attributing to God alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 12:16 as the head of this catalog instead of the tail of the preceding thesis was considered and set aside, since the refrain word reads more naturally as closing the initial claim than opening the list of named reversals.
literature_type_guess: Hymnic catalog of God reversing counselors rulers nations

boundary_rationale: A presentative particle reopens direct address to the friends: הֶן כֹּ֭ל רָאֲתָ֣ה עֵינִ֑י, “Behold, my eye has seen all this.” web:Job.13.1, and לֹא נֹפֵ֖ל אָנֹכִ֣י מִכֶּֽם, “I am not inferior to you.” web:Job.13.2, repeats the same four-word clause Job already used at Job.12.3 — consonant-identical (skeleton-tier sweep: 2 book-wide) though not byte-identical (נֹפֵ֣ל carries munach and מִכֶּ֑ם carries etnachta at Job.12.3; נֹפֵ֖ל carries tipcha and מִכֶּֽם carries meteg at Job.13.2), and verse-final only here: at Job.12.3 the same clause sits mid-verse, followed by a third colon (“Yes, who doesn't know such things as these?” web:Job.12.3). The repetition still returns the speech to the friends-address register before it pivots away again. That pivot comes at once: אוּלָ֗ם אֲ֭נִי אֶל שַׁדַּ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר וְהוֹכֵ֖חַ אֶל אֵ֣ל אֶחְפָּֽץ, rendered “I would speak to the Almighty. I desire to reason with God.” web:Job.13.3, a bicolon in which the bare consonant string אֶל appears twice as its own preposition ('to') — once governing שַׁדַּ֣י ('Shaddai') in one colon, once governing אֵ֣ל ('El', the divine name itself) in the other — parallel clauses rather than one slot holding both names in apposition (a homograph the row does not blend into any count). The indictment proper follows: וְֽאוּלָ֗ם אַתֶּ֥ם טֹֽפְלֵי שָׁ֑קֶר רֹפְאֵ֖י אֱלִ֣ל כֻּלְּכֶֽם “you are forgers of lies. You are all physicians of no value.” web:Job.13.4, including the wish מִֽי יִ֭תֵּן הַחֲרֵ֣שׁ תַּחֲרִישׁ֑וּן “Oh that you would be completely silent!” web:Job.13.5 (one of ten book-wide mi-yitten tokens, independently re-derived, kept here as texture rather than a fresh boundary since nothing else turns at this line), an imperative to reason together at 13:6, and the charge of partiality through 13:11, closing on זִֽ֭כְרֹנֵיכֶם מִשְׁלֵי אֵ֑פֶר “Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes” web:Job.13.12 before the row's own imperative shift into silence at 13:13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 13:5-12 on the strength of the mi-yitten wish at 13:5 or the imperative at 13:6 was rejected, since the whole span stays one continuous second-person indictment, closed by the ashes-and-clay image at 13:12 alone.
literature_type_guess: Job's claim of parity with friend-indictment formulation

boundary_rationale: A bare imperative opens a new address-mode: הַחֲרִ֣ישׁוּ מִ֭מֶּנִּי וַאֲדַבְּרָה אָ֑נִי “Be silent! Leave me alone, that I may speak.” web:Job.13.13, replacing the indictment of the preceding row with a command for quiet. מָ֤ה אֶשָּׂ֣א בְשָׂרִ֣י בְשִׁנָּ֑י “take my flesh in my teeth” web:Job.13.14 carries a single-witness paseq not cited as evidence. The strophe's crux is textual: at 13:15 the OSHB extract carries a ketiv/qere pair immediately adjacent, לא (ketiv) beside ל֣וֹ (qere, single-witness); the WEB rendering quoted here, הֵ֣ן יִ֭קְטְלֵנִי לא ל֣וֹ אֲיַחֵ֑ל “he will kill me. I have no hope.” web:Job.13.15, follows the ketiv reading, while the qere tradition points to a different sense - both are disclosed here without adjudicating between them. The row closes on a legal rhetorical question, מִי ה֭וּא יָרִ֣יב עִמָּדִ֑י “Who is he who will contend with me?” web:Job.13.19, still referring to God in the third person rather than addressing him directly, which is exactly what changes at the next row's opening particle.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this resolve into the preceding indictment was rejected, since the imperative here commands silence rather than continuing to name the friends' faults.
literature_type_guess: Resolve declaration with silence command fronted

boundary_rationale: A restrictive particle opens direct second-person-singular address to God, unattested earlier in this speech: אַךְ שְׁ֭תַּיִם אַל תַּ֣עַשׂ עִמָּדִ֑י “Only don't do two things to me” web:Job.13.20, immediately specified as כַּ֭פְּךָ מֵעָלַ֣י הַרְחַ֑ק “withdraw your hand far from me” web:Job.13.21. This address shift - from the friends, or from soliloquy about God in the third person, to God as direct addressee - is the strongest interior seam in this speech. The petition turns accusatory, לָֽמָּה פָנֶ֥יךָ תַסְתִּ֑יר וְתַחְשְׁבֵ֖נִי לְאוֹיֵ֣ב לָֽךְ “Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy?” web:Job.13.24, and lands in legal complaint: וְתָ֘שֵׂ֤ם בַּסַּ֨ד רַגְלַ֗י וְתִשְׁמ֥וֹר כָּל אָרְחוֹתָ֑י “You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths.” web:Job.13.27 (single-witness paseq, not cited as evidence), closing the chapter on וְ֭הוּא כְּרָקָ֣ב יִבְלֶ֑ה כְּ֝בֶ֗גֶד “I am decaying like a rotten thing” web:Job.13.28. Job.13.28 itself already opens with an explicit third-person subject, וְ֭הוּא ('and he/it', continuing the moth-eaten-garment simile), rather than the second-person address to God that carries Job.13.20-Job.13.27; this row keeps Job.13.28 on its own side of the seam because the addressee (God, second person) still governs the verse's surrounding argument and no fresh discourse frame or vocative opens elsewhere, but the person shift is a genuine crux at the row's own far edge, disclosed rather than smoothed into an unbroken second-person run. The following row's fresh universal subject, 'man' in general rather than Job's own case, opens at Job.14.1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 14:6 to keep the entire divine-address arc in one span was considered and set aside, since a fresh universal subject opens chapter 14 as its own meditation rather than continuing the personal two-requests petition.
literature_type_guess: Direct petition syntax with covenant-suit complaint

boundary_rationale: A fresh universal subject opens the row: אָ֭דָם יְל֣וּד אִשָּׁ֑ה קְצַ֥ר יָ֝מִ֗ים “Man, who is born of a woman, is of few days” web:Job.14.1, followed by כְּצִ֣יץ יָ֭צָא וַיִּמָּ֑ל “He grows up like a flower, and is cut down” web:Job.14.2, both third-person. The second-person address to God carried over from the preceding row resurfaces mid-strophe: וְאֹ֘תִ֤י תָבִ֖יא בְמִשְׁפָּ֣ט עִמָּֽךְ “bring me into judgment with you” web:Job.14.3, and מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן טָ֭הוֹר מִטָּמֵ֗א “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?” web:Job.14.4 (another of the ten book-wide mi-yitten tokens, texture here, not a fresh boundary). At 14:5 the OSHB extract carries a ketiv/qere pair adjacent, חקו (ketiv) beside חֻקָּ֥יו (qere, single-witness); Job.14.5 also carries a single-witness paseq elsewhere in the verse (inventory count alone, no word-level position encoded); the row quotes חֻקָּ֥יו עָ֝שִׂ֗יתָ וְלֹ֣א יַעֲבֽוֹר “you have appointed his bounds that he can't pass” web:Job.14.5. It closes with an imperative petition, שְׁעֵ֣ה מֵעָלָ֣יו וְיֶחְדָּ֑ל “Look away from him, that he may rest” web:Job.14.6, before an explanatory particle opens a fresh analogy in the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 14:3-6's direct address from 14:1-2's third-person description was rejected, since the whole row stays one meditation that simply moves between describing man and petitioning God about him, with no formula or vocative marking a fresh start.
literature_type_guess: Universal mortality meditation embedded within prayer

boundary_rationale: The strophe turns from Job.14.3-Job.14.6's direct petition to God — “bring me into judgment with you” web:Job.14.3, “Look away from him, that he may rest” web:Job.14.6 — back to reflective third-person analogy with no address to God at all: כִּ֤י יֵ֥שׁ לָעֵ֗ץ תִּ֫קְוָ֥ה אִֽם יִ֭כָּרֵת, “there is hope for a tree if it is cut down” web:Job.14.7. The dropped petition register, not the particle כִּ֤י itself (verse-initial כי is attested 82 times book-wide at skeleton tier -- 44 verses in the meteg-less form this verse's own opening carries and 38 verses in the meteg-bearing form כִּֽי -- and cannot alone carry a boundary) or any fresh third-person subject (Job.14.1 is already third-person), is what marks this turn. The analogy develops through מֵרֵ֣יחַ מַ֣יִם יַפְרִ֑חַ, “through the scent of water it will bud” web:Job.14.9, pivots to contrast at Job.14.10, וַיִּגְוַ֖ע אָדָ֣ם וְאַיּֽוֹ, “man gives up the spirit, and where is he?” web:Job.14.10, and closes on עַד בִּלְתִּ֣י שָׁ֭מַיִם לֹ֣א יָקִ֑יצוּ וְלֹֽא, “Until the heavens are no more, they will not awake” web:Job.14.12, before the wish-formula that opens the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping Job.14.7-Job.14.12 fused with the preceding meditation was rejected because the strophe drops the direct 2ms petition to God that governs Job.14.3-Job.14.6 and returns to reflective third-person analogy, not merely because a particle opens Job.14.7.
literature_type_guess: Nature analogy tree regeneration contrasted human death

boundary_rationale: The wish-formula opens the row: מִ֤י יִתֵּ֨ן בִּשְׁא֬וֹל תַּצְפִּנֵ֗נִי “Oh that you would hide me in Sheol” web:Job.14.13, the third of this speech's three mi-yitten tokens (after 13:5 and 14:4) and one of ten such tokens book-wide across nine verses (independently re-derived), here driving a genuine strophe boundary rather than sitting as texture. A hypothetical follows, אִם יָמ֥וּת גֶּ֗בֶר הֲיִ֫חְיֶ֥ה “If a man dies, will he live again?” web:Job.14.14, and תִּ֭קְרָא וְאָנֹכִ֣י אֶֽעֱנֶ֑ךָּ לְֽמַעֲשֵׂ֖ה “You would call, and I would answer you” web:Job.14.15 extends the wish's hopeful register before it sours: חָתֻ֣ם בִּצְר֣וֹר פִּשְׁעִ֑י וַ֝תִּטְפֹּ֗ל “My disobedience is sealed up in a bag” web:Job.14.17 reverts to complaint, closing the row before an adversative particle opens the next.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Continuing this row through 14:22 was rejected, since the adversative particle at 14:18 pivots away from the hypothetical wish register into a fresh sequence of erosion images.
literature_type_guess: Rhetorical wish for concealment and postmortem concealing

boundary_rationale: An adversative particle pivots the row open: וְ֭אוּלָם הַר נוֹפֵ֣ל יִבּ֑וֹל “the mountain falling comes to nothing” web:Job.14.18. This prefixed form (sweep: verse-initial ve-ulam, 7 book-wide, independently re-derived) is the fourth token of its particle-family inside this speech, after the bare form at 13:3 and the same prefixed form at 12:7 and 13:4 (bare ulam: 3 book-wide; the two spellings are counted separately). אֲבָנִ֤ים שָׁ֥חֲקוּ מַ֗יִם “The waters wear the stones” web:Job.14.19 (single-witness paseq) and וְתִקְוַ֖ת אֱנ֣וֹשׁ הֶאֱבַֽדְתָּ “you destroy the hope of man” web:Job.14.19 continue the erosion sequence through תִּתְקְפֵ֣הוּ לָ֭נֶצַח וַֽיַּהֲלֹ֑ךְ “You forever prevail against him, and he departs” web:Job.14.20 and יִכְבְּד֣וּ בָ֭נָיו וְלֹ֣א יֵדָ֑ע “His sons come to honor, and he doesn't know it” web:Job.14.21, closing the whole part on אַךְ בְּ֭שָׂרוֹ עָלָ֣יו יִכְאָ֑ב וְ֝נַפְשׁ֗וֹ עָלָ֥יו תֶּאֱבָֽל “his flesh on him has pain, and his soul within him mourns” web:Job.14.22.
