This is the speech's closing seam: a petuchah follows 14:22 in the Masoretic tradition (oshb:Job.14.22 (petuchah, single-witness)), and the book's next verse-initial formula is the vaya'an opening Eliphaz's second speech, “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,” web:Job.15.1 - a speaker change (Job to Eliphaz) beginning cycle two. No interior vaya'an or vayosef reopens Job's own speech anywhere between 12:1 and this close, so the mourning image at 14:22 stands as this speech's own final cadence before the formula boundary, corroborated but not driven by that mark.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row across the 14:22|15:1 seam into Eliphaz's reply was rejected outright: the vaya'an formula at 15:1 is an independently attested speaker-change marker that this speech does not cross.
literature_type_guess: Closing erosion metaphor with shadow-dissolution motif

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the verse-initial vaya'an formula that marks Eliphaz's second entry in the dialogue, וַ֭יַּעַן אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.15.1), whose gentilic הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י is spelled plene (with the extra yod), matching his earlier speech's identical spelling (הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י, oshb:Job.4.1) and distinct from the defective spelling he carries at his third speech (הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י, oshb:Job.22.1). Job's prior verse closes as a self-contained couplet, “But his flesh on him has pain, and his soul within him mourns.” (web:Job.14.22), with no address or open clause reaching across the seam, so nothing from chapter 14 belongs inside this row. Eliphaz opens his rebuke with a paired question aimed at Job's own speech, “Should a wise man answer with vain knowledge, and fill himself with the east wind?” (web:Job.15.2), continued through “Should he reason with unprofitable talk, or with speeches with which he can do no good?” (web:Job.15.3) and “Yes, you do away with fear, and hinder devotion before God.” (web:Job.15.4) to the indictment's turn against Job himself, “Your own mouth condemns you, and not I. Yes, your own lips testify against you.” (web:Job.15.6). The row closes there because 15:7 opens a new interrogative register aimed at Job's standing rather than his speech.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 14:22 into this row as a shared close for the cycle would erase the formula-marked handoff between speakers that governs every seam in the dialogue.
literature_type_guess: Eliphaz's speech opening with experiential authority claim

boundary_rationale: Eliphaz pivots from indicting Job's words to interrogating his standing, opening with “Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought out before the hills?” (web:Job.15.7) and “Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?” (web:Job.15.8). A declarative aside grounds his authority in communal seniority — גַּם שָׂ֣ב גַּם יָשִׁ֣ישׁ בָּ֑נוּ, “With us are both the gray-headed and the very aged men, much older than your father.” (web:Job.15.10) — before the interrogative mode resumes and turns to Job's temperament, “Are the consolations of God too small for you, even the word that is gentle toward you?” (web:Job.15.11). The strophe then builds an a-fortiori sequence rather than continuing as pure interrogation: the maxim מָֽה אֱנ֥וֹשׁ, “What is man, that he should be clean?” (web:Job.15.14), the presentative הֵ֣ן, “Behold, he puts no trust in his holy ones.” (web:Job.15.15) — a real particle, not an absence of one, but one that intensifies rather than opens a fresh topic — and the closing אַ֭ף כִּֽי, “how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water!” (web:Job.15.16). This mah-enosh/hen/af-ki sequence, not an unbroken run free of any particle, is what holds Job.15.7-Job.15.16 as one strophe, framed by the accusation strophe before it and the teaching-introduction formula after it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the standing-questions of 15:7-10 from the temperament-questions of 15:11-13 would carve the interrogative run at a point the Hebrew marks with no new particle or address.
literature_type_guess: Didactic principle statement divine retribution inevitability

boundary_rationale: A discourse-frame formula opens the row, אֲחַוְךָ֥ שְֽׁמַֽע לִ֑י וְזֶֽה חָ֝זִ֗יתִי וַאֲסַפֵּֽרָה (oshb:Job.15.17) (“I will show you, listen to me; that which I have seen I will declare” (web:Job.15.17)), introducing a received teaching Eliphaz credits to the fathers, “(which wise men have told by their fathers, and have not hidden it;” (web:Job.15.18) and “to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them):” (web:Job.15.19). The announced teaching itself begins at 15:20 with a fresh case-study topic, “the wicked man writhes in pain all his days, even the number of years that are laid up for the oppressor.” (web:Job.15.20), and follows the wicked man's root transgression through “Because he has stretched out his hand against God, and behaves himself proudly against the Almighty,” (web:Job.15.25) to his posture of defiance, “he runs at him with a stiff neck, with the thick shields of his bucklers,” (web:Job.15.26), and “because he has covered his face with his fatness, and gathered fat on his thighs.” (web:Job.15.27). The row holds the introduction formula together with the case study it announces rather than isolating the three-verse parenthetical, since the topic turn at Job.15.20 (a hithpolel participle, מִתְחוֹלֵ֑ל, opening the case study, not a wayyiqtol) is internal to the announced teaching. The row's own far edge at Job.15.27|Job.15.28 is not, however, a clean formal break: Job.15.27's second verb, וַיַּ֖עַשׂ ('and he made'), and Job.15.28's opening verb, וַיִּשְׁכּ֤וֹן ('and he lived'), are both wayyiqtol forms continuing one clause chain; the chain's actual break falls one verse later, at Job.15.28|Job.15.29, where the negated yiqtol form לֹֽא יֶ֭עְשַׁר interrupts it. This row keeps the seam at 15.27|15.28 anyway on topical grounds (posture of defiance giving way to consequence), disclosed here as a topical rather than a grammatical-chain boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 15:17-19 as its own row would strand a teaching-introduction formula from the very teaching it promises to deliver. Extending this row through Job.15.28 to keep the wayyiqtol chain (Job.15.27's second verb into Job.15.28's opener) intact within one row was considered; it was set aside because the topical turn to consequence at Job.15.28 still provides an adequate, if softer, seam, and the chain's grammatical break falls at Job.15.28|Job.15.29 regardless of where the row edge sits at 15.27|15.28.
literature_type_guess: Ancestral exemplar catalog of the wicked's transgression

boundary_rationale: The row turns from the wicked man's posture of defiance to the consequence that follows it, “He has lived in desolate cities, in houses which no one inhabited, which were ready to become heaps.” (web:Job.15.28), through the loss of substance, “He will not be rich, neither will his substance continue, neither will their possessions be extended on the earth.” (web:Job.15.29), and the warning against trusting emptiness, “Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his reward.” (web:Job.15.31), closing on the harvest of that emptiness, “They conceive mischief and produce iniquity. Their heart prepares deceit.” (web:Job.15.35). A paragraph mark in this stretch follows this closing verse, oshb:Job.15.35 (samekh, single-witness), a weak corroboration for the edge that the following verse-initial vaya'an formula at 16:1 already carries on its own. Eliphaz's speech ends here without a colophon or further address, so the row's close is also the speech's close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 16:1 would fold a new speaker's formula into the wicked man's poem despite the speech boundary the vaya'an formula itself marks. Moving this row's near edge earlier, to keep the Job.15.27|Job.15.28 wayyiqtol chain inside one row, was considered; it is not adopted here since the chain's own break falls at Job.15.28|Job.15.29 regardless, and the topical turn to consequence at Job.15.28 still marks a defensible, if softer, seam.
literature_type_guess: Vivid description wicked's terror during death hour

boundary_rationale: Job's reply opens on its own verse-initial formula, וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.16.1), the same vaya'an-plus-frame pattern that opens each of his replies across the cycle. He turns Eliphaz's charge of empty speech back on him at once, “I have heard many such things. You are all miserable comforters!” (web:Job.16.2), and “Shall vain words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?” (web:Job.16.3), before a conditional reversal of roles, “I also could speak as you do. If your soul were in my soul's place, I could join words together against you, and shake my head at you,” (web:Job.16.4), followed by “but I would strengthen you with my mouth. The solace of my lips would relieve you.” (web:Job.16.5), closing the retort on the solace he claims he would have offered them. This opening unit ends before 16:6 turns from addressing the friends to a reflection with no named addressee at all.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this retort past 16:5 into the following reflection would blend Job's address to the friends with the address shift toward the divine that follows immediately.
literature_type_guess: Job's second-cycle response opening to miserable comforters

boundary_rationale: The row turns from Job's retort to the friends toward his own unrelieved suffering: אִֽם אֲ֭דַבְּרָה לֹא יֵחָשֵׂ֣ךְ כְּאֵבִ֑י, “Though I speak, my grief is not subsided.” (web:Job.16.6), a reflective clause naming no addressee at all; its verb יֵחָשֵׂ֣ךְ shares its root with Job.16.5's closing יַחְשֹֽׂךְ (qal there, niphal here — a real lexical bond across the 16.5|16.6 seam, disclosed rather than left implicit, though it does not by itself move either row's edge). Job.16.7 is grammatically mixed, not uniformly second-person: its opening verb, הֶלְאָ֑נִי, is third-person ('he has wearied me'), and just its second verb, הֲ֝שִׁמּ֗וֹתָ ('you have made desolate'), is 2ms; the Hebrew names no addressee at all here — 'God' is WEB's own supplied vocative, not present in the text (“But now, God, you have surely worn me out. You have made all my company desolate.” web:Job.16.7). The unambiguous second-person address that this row's device rests on is Job.16.8's own opening wayyiqtol, וַֽ֭תִּקְמְטֵנִי ('you have shriveled me up'), continued in “This is a witness against me. My leanness rises up against me. It testifies to my face.” (web:Job.16.8). This singular, unnamed address is a distinct discourse mode from the plural friends-address at Job.16.2-Job.16.5 (itself narrowing once, at Job.16.3, to a lone 2ms addressee — disclosed there), and it gives way in turn to third-person description at Job.16.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping Job.16.6-Job.16.8 inside the retort to the friends would erase this row's own shift: the friends are addressed as a group at Job.16.2, Job.16.4, and Job.16.5 (with one narrowing to a lone addressee at Job.16.3, disclosed at Job.16.2-Job.16.5); Job.16.6 drops any addressee, and Job.16.8 opens address to a new, unnamed singular addressee distinct from the friends. The contrast that grounds this row's near edge is the addressee's identity — friends, then no one, then an unnamed 'you' — not verb number alone.
literature_type_guess: Sighing-groaning lament with direct God-complaint syntax

boundary_rationale: The row shifts from direct second-person address to third-person description of an assailant, “He has torn me in his wrath and persecuted me. He has gnashed on me with his teeth. My adversary sharpens his eyes on me.” (web:Job.16.9), through the crowd's mockery, “They have gaped on me with their mouth. They have struck me on the cheek reproachfully. They gather themselves together against me.” (web:Job.16.10), and the accusation against God directly, “God delivers me to the ungodly, and casts me into the hands of the wicked.” (web:Job.16.11), to a run of violent images closing on “He breaks me with breach on breach. He runs at me like a giant.” (web:Job.16.14). This third-person description of assault is a distinct register from both the retort to the friends and the singular address that precede it, and it gives way to Job's own self-description of mourning at 16:15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this assault sequence with the mourning-ritual verses that follow would blend third-person description of what has been done to Job with his own direct response to it.
literature_type_guess: Divine violence account personified assault metaphor

boundary_rationale: Job turns from describing the assault to his own response to it, fronting the object of his mourning ritual: שַׂ֣ק תָּ֭פַרְתִּי עֲלֵ֣י גִלְדִּ֑י, “I have sewed sackcloth on my skin, and have thrust my horn in the dust.” (web:Job.16.15), continued in his physical distress, “My face is red with weeping. Deep darkness is on my eyelids,” (web:Job.16.16), and closing on a protest of innocence, “although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.” (web:Job.16.17). The preceding row's own opening also fronts a term before its verb (שָׁ֘לֵ֤ו הָיִ֨יתִי, 'I was at ease,' Job.16.12), so word order alone does not distinguish this row's edge; what changes at Job.16.15 is Job's grammatical role, from the described object of a third-person assault (Job.16.9-Job.16.14) to the grammatical subject of his own 1cs acts (שַׂ֣ק תָּ֭פַרְתִּי, 'I have sewed') — a participant-role shift, not the fronting by itself, marks the topic turn to Job's own mourning and innocence, a short unit that ends before the vocative apostrophe to the earth opens the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 16:15-17 as a continuation of the assault sequence would miss the fronted object that marks Job's own response as a new topic.
literature_type_guess: Weeping into dust with face-transformation imagery

boundary_rationale: A vocative apostrophe opens the row, אֶ֭רֶץ אַל תְּכַסִּ֣י דָמִ֑י וְֽאַל יְהִ֥י מָ֝ק֗וֹם לְזַעֲקָתִֽי (oshb:Job.16.18) (“Earth, don't cover my blood. Let my cry have no place to rest.” (web:Job.16.18)), addressing the ground itself rather than the friends or the divine. The row continues on a 'behold'-headed clause, “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven. He who vouches for me is on high.” (web:Job.16.19), through the friends' scorn, “My friends scoff at me. My eyes pour out tears to God,” (web:Job.16.20), the appeal itself, “that he would maintain the right of a man with God, of a son of man with his neighbor!” (web:Job.16.21), and closes on the approach of death: כִּֽי שְׁנ֣וֹת מִסְפָּ֣ר יֶאֱתָ֑יוּ וְאֹ֖רַח לֹא אָשׁ֣וּב אֶהֱלֹֽךְ (“For when a few years have come, I will go the way of no return.” web:Job.16.22), a ki-headed clause carrying its own finite verb pair. The next verse opens a new, asyndetic clause with a fresh subject and predicate sharing no verb with 16:22 — רוּחִ֣י חֻ֭בָּלָה יָמַ֥י נִזְעָ֗כוּ קְבָרִ֥ים לִֽי (“My spirit is consumed. My days are extinct and the grave is ready for me.” web:Job.17.1). The row crosses the chapter number on topic and address continuity alone: both verses share one mortality theme and no new addressee, formula, or particle intervenes between them, even though they are two grammatically separate clauses rather than one continuous sentence; the next shift comes at 17:2's oath-headed turn to the mockers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking this row at the chapter number between 16:22 and 17:1 would impose a metadata division at a point where topic and address run unbroken, even though the two verses are grammatically distinct clauses (16:22 ki-headed with its own verb pair; 17:1 asyndetic with a fresh subject and predicate) rather than one continuous sentence.
literature_type_guess: Blood-crying witness and advocate-seeking legal formulation

boundary_rationale: An oath-type asseverative particle opens the row, אִם לֹ֣א הֲ֭תֻלִים עִמָּדִ֑י וּ֝בְהַמְּרוֹתָ֗ם תָּלַ֥ן עֵינִֽי (oshb:Job.17.2) (“Surely there are mockers with me. My eye dwells on their provocation.” (web:Job.17.2)), turning from the mortality clause just closed to a fresh complaint. The register shifts again to direct imperative petition, “Now give a pledge. Be collateral for me with yourself. Who is there who will strike hands with me?” (web:Job.17.3), before Job indicts the friends' understanding, “For you have hidden their heart from understanding, therefore you will not exalt them.” (web:Job.17.4), and closes on a curse-form judgment against betrayal, “He who denounces his friends for plunder, even the eyes of his children will fail.” (web:Job.17.5). The row ends there because 17:6 opens a new topic on Job's public shame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 17:2 to the death-wish unit before it would pass over the asseverative particle that opens a fresh complaint rather than continuing the mortality clause.
literature_type_guess: Bargain petition for witness-advocate among the dead

boundary_rationale: The row turns to Job's public humiliation, “But he has made me a byword of the people. They spit in my face.” (web:Job.17.6), and its physical toll, “My eye also is dim by reason of sorrow. All my members are as a shadow.” (web:Job.17.7), before pivoting to how the upright react to it, “Upright men will be astonished at this. The innocent will stir himself up against the godless.” (web:Job.17.8), and closing on a maxim of perseverance, “Yet the righteous will hold to his way. He who has clean hands will grow stronger and stronger.” (web:Job.17.9). This shame-to-maxim unit is a distinct topic from both the pledge-appeal before it and the direct address to the friends that reopens at 17:10.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 17:6-9 as part of the pledge-appeal unit would miss the topic turn from a legal request to Job's public shame and the maxim that answers it.
literature_type_guess: Contempt-from-humans catalog with complete orphaning state

boundary_rationale: The row opens on a direct address shift back to the friends, וְֽאוּלָ֗ם כֻּלָּ֣ם תָּ֭שֻׁבוּ וּבֹ֣אוּ נָ֑א וְלֹֽא אֶמְצָ֖א בָכֶ֣ם חָכָֽם (oshb:Job.17.10) (“But as for you all, come back. I will not find a wise man among you.” (web:Job.17.10)), a plural imperative that returns to the addressee of Job's opening retort after several rows of third-person and singular address. Job then turns to his own hopelessness, “My days are past. My plans are broken off, as are the thoughts of my heart.” (web:Job.17.11), through the death-imagery of “If I look for Sheol as my house, if I have spread my couch in the darkness,” (web:Job.17.13) and “if I have said to corruption, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' and 'My sister,'” (web:Job.17.14), closing on “Shall it go down with me to the gates of Sheol, or descend together into the dust?” (web:Job.17.16). A paragraph mark follows this closing verse, oshb:Job.17.16 (samekh, single-witness), and Bildad's own vaya'an formula opens the very next verse, וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשֻּׁחִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.18.1), so the row's close coincides with the seam between Job's reply and Bildad's second speech: the formula-marked handoff to Bildad begins cleanly at Job.18.1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row into 18:1 would carry Job's speech across the vaya'an formula that both the dialogue's formula spine and the paragraph mark at 17:16 treat as its close.
literature_type_guess: Underworld meditation with torch-extinguishing finality

boundary_rationale: The seam at Job.17.16|Job.18.1 is a clean speech boundary: Job's cycle-two reply closes on “Shall it go down with me to the gates of Sheol,” (web:Job.17.16) before Bildad's second speech opens with the vaya'an formula, וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשֻּׁחִ֗י (oshb:Job.18.1) — spelling the gentilic defectively, unlike the full spelling וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשּׁוּחִ֗י that opens his earlier speech (web:Job.8.1). The formula runs straight into a rebuke launched by the two-word interrogative עַד אָ֤נָה (“How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and afterwards we will speak.”, web:Job.18.2); the same two-word skeleton reopens at the head of Job's own reply, עַד אָ֭נָה (web:Job.19.2), though the two verses' accents differ (mahpakh here at 18:2, dehi at 19:2), so the pairing holds at the accent-stripped tier rather than as a byte-identical repeat. Bildad presses the friends' collective standing (“Why are we counted as animals, which have become unclean in your sight?”, web:Job.18.3) before turning the rebuke on Job's anger directly: הַ֭לְמַעַנְךָ (“You who tear yourself in your anger,” web:Job.18.4) carries the 2ms suffix, narrowing the address from the 2mp forms of 18:2-18:3; the address breaks off again at web:Job.18.5, where the grammatical subject shifts to the generic third-person class of the wicked.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the formula verse web:Job.18.1 as a row by itself was rejected because no signal separates it from the interrogative address it introduces.
literature_type_guess: Bildad's indignant response opening impatience declaration

boundary_rationale: At web:Job.18.5 the address pivots from second-person “you” to third-person description, opened by the particle-headed clause גַּ֤ם א֣וֹר רְשָׁעִ֣ים יִדְעָ֑ךְ (“Yes, the light of the wicked will be put out.” web:Job.18.5) introducing “the wicked” as a new grammatical subject one verse after the 2nd-person singular suffix of Job.18.4 (הַ֭לְמַעַנְךָ) had already narrowed the friends' plural address of Job.18.2-Job.18.3 to Job alone; Bildad no longer addresses Job directly but recites the fate of the wicked as a class. The strophe then develops one image-chain cataloging the wicked man's downfall across six verses, though the grammatical subject varies image by image: light and lamp govern Job.18.5-Job.18.6, his own steps and counsel govern Job.18.7, the man himself is subject in exactly 1 of the 6 verses -- Job.18.8 alone -- (“he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he wanders into its mesh” web:Job.18.8), and trap and snare become the subject at Job.18.9-Job.18.10; the catalog runs through Job.18.10 before web:Job.18.11 introduces terrors as a new active subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the net-and-snare verses web:Job.18.8-Job.18.10 into their own row was rejected because the catalog format opened by גַּ֤ם at 18:5 runs unbroken through 18:10 with no new address-shift or formula inside it, even though the catalog's own grammatical subject varies image by image rather than staying fixed on the wicked man's feet.
literature_type_guess: Light-to-darkness metaphor describing wicked's punishment

boundary_rationale: The strophe is bounded by its own inclusio: סָ֭בִיב בִּֽעֲתֻ֣הוּ בַלָּה֑וֹת (“Terrors will make him afraid on every side,” web:Job.18.11) reappears at its close in the shorter form לְמֶ֣לֶךְ בַּלָּהֽוֹת (“He will be brought to the king of terrors.” web:Job.18.14) — the same word for terrors framing both edges of a four-verse unit that also marks its own subject shift, since terrors and calamity (web:Job.18.11-Job.18.12), not the man's own feet, now govern the verbs. The devouring disease of web:Job.18.13 escalates toward the personified king of terrors who leads him away in web:Job.18.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding these four verses into the trap imagery before them or the estate-ruin catalog after them was rejected because the recurring word for “terrors” marks the unit as its own strophe.
literature_type_guess: Layered trap and snare metaphor for wicked's capture

boundary_rationale: The catalog turns from the man's body to his household and memory: the tent named a verse earlier at Job.18.14 (מֵ֭אָהֳלוֹ, from which he is uprooted) now receives a new occupant — something “which is none of his” — תִּשְׁכּ֣וֹן בְּ֭אָהֳלוֹ (web:Job.18.15); his roots and branch are cut off (web:Job.18.16), and his memory perishes “His memory will perish from the earth. He will have no name in the street.” (web:Job.18.17); he is driven from the world with neither son nor grandson nor survivor among his people (web:Job.18.18-Job.18.19). Onlookers reacting עַל י֭וֹמוֹ נָשַׁ֣מּוּ אַחֲרֹנִ֑ים וְ֝קַדְמֹנִ֗ים אָ֣חֲזוּ שָֽׂעַר (“Those who come after will be astonished at his day, as those who went before were frightened.”, web:Job.18.20) lead into Bildad's own summarizing tag, אַךְ אֵ֭לֶּה מִשְׁכְּנ֣וֹת עַוָּ֑ל (“Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous.”, web:Job.18.21) — a demonstrative that gathers up the whole catalog before the speech ends; a setumah follows web:Job.18.21 in the Masoretic tradition (oshb:Job.18.21 (setumah, single-witness)).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking off the onlookers' reaction at web:Job.18.20-Job.18.21 as its own row was rejected because Bildad's closing demonstrative still gathers up the entire estate-and-memory catalog rather than opening fresh material.
literature_type_guess: Desolate-dwelling and premature-death consequence description

boundary_rationale: Job's reply opens with the vaya'an formula (web:Job.19.1) and immediately reopens Bildad's own two-word interrogative in kind: עַד אָ֭נָה תּוֹגְי֣וּן נַפְשִׁ֑י וּֽתְדַכְּאוּנַ֥נִי בְמִלִּֽים (“How long will you torment me, and crush me with words?”, web:Job.19.2) — the skeleton עד אנה is otherwise unattested in the book (sweep: 2 book-wide, Job.18.2 and Job.19.2 only), though the two verses' cantillation differs (dehi here at 19:2 against mahpakh at 18:2), so the reopening holds at the accent-stripped tier rather than as a byte-identical repetition of Bildad's opener at web:Job.18.2. Job protests the friends' repeated reproach (web:Job.19.3) and disclaims responsibility even where he may have erred (web:Job.19.4), then states the terms of the exchange as a conditional: אִם אָ֭מְנָם עָלַ֣י תַּגְדִּ֑ילוּ וְתוֹכִ֥יחוּ עָ֝לַ֗י חֶרְפָּתִּֽי (“If indeed you will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach,”, web:Job.19.5) sets a protasis whose apodosis follows at web:Job.19.6, דְּֽעוּ אֵ֭פוֹ כִּי אֱל֣וֹהַּ עִוְּתָ֑נִי וּ֝מְצוּד֗וֹ עָלַ֥י הִקִּֽיף (“know now that God has subverted me, and has surrounded me with his net.”) — the protasis-apodosis pair closes the opening unit before web:Job.19.7 turns to a new complaint introduced by הֵ֤ן.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Job.19.1 as a bare formula row apart from the following address was rejected because no independent signal marks a break before the interrogative that the formula verse itself introduces.
literature_type_guess: Job's third-cycle response opening with indignant rebuke

boundary_rationale: הֵ֤ן אֶצְעַ֣ק חָ֭מָס (“Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard.”, web:Job.19.7) opens a fresh strophe with the topic-turn particle הֵ֤ן, introducing Job's complaint that his cry for help goes unanswered. God stands as the unstated subject of every main verb through Job.19.8-Job.19.10 — he has walled Job's way (web:Job.19.8, with Job's own consequential 1cs אֶעֱב֑וֹר, 'I cannot pass,' inside the same verse), stripped his glory (web:Job.19.9), “broken me down on every side” like an uprooted tree (web:Job.19.10, with Job's own consequential 1cs וָאֵלַ֑ךְ, 'and I am gone,' inside the same verse) — but the mediating agent shifts at the clause level from Job.19.11 on: its opening clause, וַיַּ֣חַר עָלַ֣י אַפּ֑וֹ (“He has also kindled his wrath against me.” web:Job.19.11), takes 'his anger' (אַפּ֑וֹ) as its expressed subject, and Job.19.12's siege image runs entirely on גְדוּדָ֗יו ('his troops') as the expressed 3mp subject of all three of its verbs — “His troops come on together, build a siege ramp against me, and encamp around my tent.” (web:Job.19.12). The unit still closes as one divine-assault movement before web:Job.19.13 turns to human abandonment.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the siege imagery through web:Job.19.13 was rejected because a participant shift begins there: colon A (אַ֭חַי מֵעָלַ֣י הִרְחִ֑יק) resumes the divine-assault chain's unstated 3ms subject after the expressed mediating subjects of Job.19.11-Job.19.12, with 'my brothers' as its object alone, but colon B (וְ֝יֹדְעַ֗י אַךְ זָ֥רוּ מִמֶּֽנִּי) names 'my acquaintances' as the roster's earliest expressed human subject — the shift completes within the verse rather than at its opening word.
literature_type_guess: Accusation of cosmic violence and suppressed justice-seeking

boundary_rationale: The strophe catalogs Job's social abandonment in place of the divine-assault imagery just closed. Job.19.13 itself turns gradually: its opening colon, אַ֭חַי מֵעָלַ֣י הִרְחִ֑יק (“He has put my brothers far from me.” web:Job.19.13), resumes the divine-assault chain's unstated 3ms subject after the expressed mediating subjects of Job.19.11-Job.19.12, naming 'my brothers' as object alone; the roster's earliest expressed human subject arrives in the verse's second colon, וְ֝יֹדְעַ֗י אַךְ זָ֥רוּ מִמֶּֽנִּי (“My acquaintances are wholly estranged from me.” web:Job.19.13). From there the roster names relatives and familiar friends who withdraw (web:Job.19.14); houseguests and maids treat him as a stranger (web:Job.19.15), Job himself becomes the roster's earliest acting grammatical subject at its servant item, לְעַבְדִּ֣י קָ֭רָאתִי (“I call to my servant,” web:Job.19.16) — one verse after 19:15's closing colon, נָ֝כְרִ֗י הָיִ֥יתִי בְעֵינֵיהֶֽם, already names his own state (“I am an alien in their sight.” web:Job.19.15) — his breath repels his wife and his mother's sons (web:Job.19.17), even children despise him (web:Job.19.18), and the men of his intimate circle turn against him (web:Job.19.19). The roster closes on the proverbial image of web:Job.19.20, “I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.” (וָ֝אֶתְמַלְּטָ֗ה בְּע֣וֹר שִׁנָּֽי), before the direct plea of web:Job.19.21 shifts back into second-person address.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the household members of web:Job.19.13-Job.19.15 from the servant-and-family verses that follow was set aside because the roster reads as one continuous accumulation of estrangement despite an internal shift: לְעַבְדִּ֣י קָ֭רָאתִי (“I call to my servant,” web:Job.19.16) is the roster's earliest clause where Job himself, not those around him, becomes the acting grammatical subject (1cs), one verse after 19:15's closing 1cs copula הָיִ֥יתִי already names his own state.
literature_type_guess: Progressive isolation catalog family strangers servants estrangement

boundary_rationale: Job turns from cataloging his abandonment to direct address, doubling the imperative in חָנֻּ֬נִי חָנֻּ֣נִי אַתֶּ֣ם רֵעָ֑י (“Have pity on me. Have pity on me, you my friends”, web:Job.19.21) — the repeated verb marks the strophe's own emphatic opening, appealing to the hand of God that has touched him. Job.19.22 continues the same second-person address, asking why the friends persecute him as God and are not satisfied with his flesh, before web:Job.19.23 pivots to the wish-formula מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן and a different register entirely.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this plea into the preceding catalog of estrangement was rejected because the doubled imperative and second-person address mark a distinct rhetorical turn rather than a further catalog item.
literature_type_guess: Plea for pity formulation hand-striking gesture invocation

boundary_rationale: The wish-formula מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן opens the strophe twice within one verse, מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן אֵ֭פוֹ וְיִכָּתְב֣וּן מִלָּ֑י מִֽי יִתֵּ֖ן בַּסֵּ֣פֶר וְיֻחָֽקוּ (“Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!”, web:Job.19.23) — the doubled topic-turn interrogative launching Job's wish for a permanent record, developed through the iron pen and rock of web:Job.19.24. The strophe turns from wish to declaration at web:Job.19.25, וַאֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי גֹּ֣אֲלִי חָ֑י (“I know that my Redeemer lives.”), and closes on the emotional summation of web:Job.19.27, כָּל֖וּ כִלְיֹתַ֣י בְּחֵקִֽי (“My heart is consumed within me.”), before web:Job.19.28 pivots to a hypothetical warning addressed to the friends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Dividing the wish for a written record at web:Job.19.23-Job.19.24 from the Redeemer declaration at web:Job.19.25-Job.19.27 into separate rows was rejected because both halves develop one continuous hope for future vindication with no intervening address-shift or formula.
literature_type_guess: Testimony-inscription appeal with vindication witness beyond death

boundary_rationale: כִּ֣י תֹ֭אמְרוּ (“If you say, ‘How we will persecute him!’”, web:Job.19.28) opens a quotation frame anticipating the friends' own hostile words, pivoting from Job's declaration of hope back to a warning addressed to them; the closing couplet, “be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishments of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment.” (web:Job.19.29), warns of judgment. The verse's final word carries a ketiv/qere pair adjacent in the text, לְמַ֖עַן תֵּדְע֣וּן שדין שַׁדּֽוּן (single-witness, oshb:Job.19.29), and a setumah follows Job.19.29 in the Masoretic tradition (oshb:Job.19.29 (setumah, single-witness)) at the close of Job's reply, before Zophar's own vaya'an formula opens web:Job.20.1, “Then Zophar the Naamathite answered,”
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this closing warning to the Redeemer strophe at web:Job.19.23-Job.19.27 was rejected because the quotation frame כִּ֣י תֹ֭אמְרוּ opens a distinct hypothetical address to the friends rather than continuing Job's declaration of hope.
literature_type_guess: Warning-to-friends against complicity in divine violence

boundary_rationale: Zophar's second speech opens with the verse-initial formula וַ֭יַּעַן צֹפַ֥ר הַנַּֽעֲמָתִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר “Then Zophar the Naamathite answered,” web:Job.20.1 — the second of only two Zophar tokens in the vaya'an inventory (sweep: 2 book-wide, Job.11.1 and Job.20.1; no third Zophar speech follows anywhere in the cycle). Rather than turning at once to Job, Zophar accounts for his own agitation before addressing Job: לָ֭כֵן שְׂעִפַּ֣י יְשִׁיב֑וּנִי “Therefore my thoughts answer me,” web:Job.20.2, continuing through מוּסַ֣ר כְּלִמָּתִ֣י אֶשְׁמָ֑ע “I have heard the reproof which puts me to shame.” web:Job.20.3. This self-referential motive clause closes out before the interrogative that opens the next strophe at 20:4, so the speech formula and its preface hold together as one short unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 20:1 as a bare narrator tag apart from 20:2-3 would sever the formula from the very agitation it introduces.
literature_type_guess: Zophar's second-cycle response opening with restraint-breaking

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the strophe: הֲזֹ֣את יָ֭דַעְתָּ מִנִּי עַ֑ד מִנִּ֤י שִׂ֖ים אָדָ֣ם עֲלֵי אָֽרֶץ “Don’t you know this from old time, since man was placed on earth,” web:Job.20.4, launching Zophar's thesis that the wicked's triumph is brief. The description proceeds in concessive form — אִם יַעֲלֶ֣ה לַשָּׁמַ֣יִם שִׂיא֑וֹ “Though his height mount up to the heavens” web:Job.20.6 — through the simile of a dream that flies away (20:8) and the man nobody can find again (20:9), down to his own household: בָּ֭נָיו יְרַצּ֣וּ דַלִּ֑ים וְ֝יָדָ֗יו תָּשֵׁ֥בְנָה אוֹנֽוֹ (“His children will seek the favor of the poor. His hands will give back his wealth.” web:Job.20.10) — restitution and favor-seeking, not yet the specific charge of prior oppression that the speech states only later at web:Job.20.19 — and עַ֭צְמוֹתָיו מָלְא֣וּ עלומו עֲלוּמָ֑יו וְ֝עִמּ֗וֹ עַל עָפָ֥ר תִּשְׁכָּֽב, crossing a ketiv/qere pair (single-witness), “His bones are full of his youth, but youth will lie down with him in the dust.” web:Job.20.11. The unit runs from the opening question to this image of burial, before a fresh concessive clause turns to a new figure — sin swallowed like food — at 20:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking 20:10-11 off into their own decision would isolate the household coda from the collapse it completes.
literature_type_guess: Ancestral-origin and time-bound wicked's fleeting joy

boundary_rationale: A second concessive clause opens the strophe: אִם תַּמְתִּ֣יק בְּפִ֣יו רָעָ֑ה יַ֝כְחִידֶ֗נָּה תַּ֣חַת לְשׁוֹנֽוֹ “Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue,” web:Job.20.12, launching the image of sin as food that will not stay down. The description brackets itself with the same word for venom: מְרוֹרַ֖ת פְּתָנִ֣ים בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ “It is cobra venom within him.” web:Job.20.14 and, two verses later, רֹאשׁ פְּתָנִ֥ים יִינָ֑ק “He will suck cobra venom.” web:Job.20.16 (skeleton פתנים — sweep: 2 book-wide, both members inside this span, Job.20.14 and Job.20.16; the two pointed forms are themselves each a byte-singleton — munach at 20:14 against merkha at 20:16 — so the inclusio holds at the consonantal tier, not as a repeated pointed string). The same skeleton דלים ('poor') that closes this span at web:Job.20.19 already appears two verses before the span opens, at web:Job.20.10 (skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide, Job.20.10, Job.20.19, Job.31.16), with Job.20.11 intervening and carrying no דלים member — a repetition straddling this row's opening seam at 20:11|20:12 across that empty intervening verse, disclosed here; the root-level רצץ, by contrast, sweeps only 1 book-wide (Job.20.19 itself; 20:10's own verb is a different root), so no root-level bracket is separately claimable and the דלים lexical pair is the whole of the cross-seam signal. The second half turns from poison to profit — the streams of honey he will not see (20:17), the gain he must restore (20:18) — and closes on its cause: כִּֽי רִ֭צַּץ עָזַ֣ב דַּלִּ֑ים “For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor.” web:Job.20.19, before a fresh causal clause opens the next strophe at 20:20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting between the venom image and the honey-and-restitution image at Job.20.16|Job.20.17 was rejected not because it would sever the פתנים inclusio — both members (Job.20.14, Job.20.16) already sit on the same side of that cut, so the device is closed before the proposed seam — but because the sin-as-food figure that opens the strophe at Job.20.12 (wickedness sweet in his mouth) continues past the venom that replaces that sweetness at Job.20.14 and Job.20.16 into the honey he will not see at Job.20.17 and the gain he must restore, unswallowed, at Job.20.18, giving the span its real closing edge at Job.20.19, where the causal clause כִּֽי רִ֭צַּץ עָזַ֣ב דַּלִּ֑ים names its cause, not at Job.20.16.
literature_type_guess: Ingestion metaphor corruption from within bowels toxin

boundary_rationale: A causal clause opens this final strophe of Zophar's speech: כִּ֤י לֹא יָדַ֣ע שָׁלֵ֣ו בְּבִטְנ֑וֹ “Because he knew no quietness within him,” web:Job.20.20, and the description of unrelieved distress runs through the rain of divine wrath while he is eating (20:23), the flight from the weapon — יִ֭בְרַח מִנֵּ֣שֶׁק בַּרְזֶ֑ל “He will flee from the iron weapon.” web:Job.20.24 — the unfanned fire in his tent (20:26), and the heavens and earth testifying against him (20:27), before the speech closes on its own summary formula: זֶ֤ה חֵֽלֶק אָדָ֣ם רָ֭שָׁע מֵאֱלֹהִ֑ים “This is the portion of a wicked man from God,” web:Job.20.29. A PE follows 20:29 (oshb:Job.20.29 (petuchah, single-witness)), corroborating the close of Zophar's speech at exactly this gnomic summary, immediately before Job's own vaya'an formula opens the reply at 21:1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Peeling 20:24-29 into a decision of its own would strand the weapon-and-fire imagery from the distress that provokes it in 20:20-23.
literature_type_guess: Choking vomit-recovery and divine-forced regurgitation syntax

boundary_rationale: Job's reply opens with his own vaya'an formula, וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר “Then Job answered,” web:Job.21.1, immediately followed by a direct appeal to the friends: וּתְהִי זֹ֝֗את תַּנְח֥וּמֹֽתֵיכֶֽם “Let this be your consolation.” web:Job.21.2, asking to be allowed to finish before they mock (21:3). Job then turns the complaint back on himself — הֶ֭אָנֹכִי לְאָדָ֣ם שִׂיחִ֑י “As for me, is my complaint to man?” web:Job.21.4 — and closes the appeal on his own dread: וְאִם זָכַ֥רְתִּי וְנִבְהָ֑לְתִּי “When I remember, I am troubled.” web:Job.21.6. This appeal-and-dread unit ends before the fresh interrogative that states Job's actual thesis at 21:7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the formula in 21:1 from the appeal in 21:2-6 would leave the plea for a hearing without its speaker.
literature_type_guess: Job's fourth-cycle response opening with listening demand

boundary_rationale: The chapter's governing question opens the strophe: מַדּ֣וּעַ רְשָׁעִ֣ים יִחְי֑וּ עָ֝תְק֗וּ גַּם גָּ֥בְרוּ חָֽיִל “Why do the wicked live, become old, yes, and grow mighty in power?” web:Job.21.7, directly answering the premise of Zophar's speech that the wicked's triumph is brief. The catalogue that follows describes the opposite: children established before their eyes (21:8), houses safe from fear (21:9), thriving livestock (21:10), and singing children (21:11-12), until the strophe closes on their peaceful end: “They spend their days in prosperity. In an instant they go down to Sheol.” web:Job.21.13. The unit runs from the thesis question to this summary of an untroubled death, before a quotation frame opens the next strophe at 21:14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Stopping the strophe at 21:11 to isolate the children's dancing would break the prosperity catalogue before its own conclusion in 21:13.
literature_type_guess: Empirical observation of wicked's robust flourishing prosperity

boundary_rationale: A quotation frame breaks in: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ לָ֭אֵל ס֣וּר מִמֶּ֑נּוּ וְדַ֥עַת דְּ֝רָכֶ֗יךָ לֹ֣א חָפָֽצְנוּ “They tell God, ‘Depart from us, for we don’t want to know about your ways.” web:Job.21.14, the wicked's own words continuing through their dismissal of the Almighty in 21:15. Job does not endorse this speech; he sets it at arm's length: הֵ֤ן לֹ֣א בְיָדָ֣ם טוּבָ֑ם עֲצַ֥ת רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים רָ֣חֲקָה מֶֽנִּי “Behold, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the wicked is far from me.” web:Job.21.16. The quoted impiety and Job's disclaiming aside form one short strophe, closing before the fresh interrogative at 21:17 turns to the timing of judgment.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 21:14-16 into the prosperity catalogue above would blur the shift from Job's own description to the wicked's quoted voice.
literature_type_guess: Wicked's deliberate distance from God yet material thriving

boundary_rationale: A second interrogative opens this strophe, echoing the pattern set at 21:7: כַּמָּ֤ה נֵר רְשָׁ֘עִ֤ים יִדְעָ֗ךְ “How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out,” web:Job.21.17, challenging the friends to say how regularly the wicked actually suffer. Job goes on to challenge the claim that God simply defers judgment onto a man's children. The whole of Job.21.19 reads as one unbroken third-person statement in the Hebrew — אֱל֗וֹהַּ יִצְפֹּן לְבָנָ֥יו אוֹנ֑וֹ יְשַׁלֵּ֖ם אֵלָ֣יו וְיֵדָֽע, with no quotative particle or speech-root verb anywhere in the verse (contrast וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ opening the friends' own quoted claim at Job.21.14, and כִּ֤י תֹֽאמְר֗וּ opening a second quoted claim at Job.21.28). WEB nonetheless supplies an interpretive break: “You say, 'God lays up his iniquity for his children.' Let him recompense it to himself, that he may know it.” (web:Job.21.19). Read as the Hebrew gives it, with no such break in the source, Job states the deferred-judgment premise and its rebuttal as one continuous claim. The strophe closes on the man's own indifference once his months are cut off (21:21).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this strophe with the death material next door would run the deferred-punishment argument together with a separate parity-in-death argument.
literature_type_guess: Wicked's dynasty and offspring thriving with celebration

boundary_rationale: A third interrogative turns the argument again: הַלְאֵ֥ל יְלַמֶּד דָּ֑עַת “Shall any teach God knowledge,” web:Job.21.22, introducing a pair of deaths that receive identical treatment regardless of their circumstances — one dies “in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet.” web:Job.21.23, another dies “in bitterness of soul, and never tastes of good.” web:Job.21.25. The strophe closes on their shared grave: יַ֭חַד עַל עָפָ֣ר יִשְׁכָּ֑בוּ וְ֝רִמָּ֗ה תְּכַסֶּ֥ה עֲלֵיהֶֽם “They lie down alike in the dust. The worm covers them.” web:Job.21.26, before Job turns to address the friends directly again at 21:27.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe into the closing address would erase the return to direct second-person speech that marks the next unit.
literature_type_guess: Rhetorical why-questions on divine non-intervention delays

boundary_rationale: Direct address returns to close the chapter: הֵ֣ן יָ֭דַעְתִּי מַחְשְׁבֽוֹתֵיכֶ֑ם וּ֝מְזִמּ֗וֹת עָלַ֥י תַּחְמֹֽסוּ “Behold, I know your thoughts, the plans with which you would wrong me.” web:Job.21.27, answering the claim Job puts in the friends' own mouths — “Where is the house of the prince?” web:Job.21.28 — with an appeal to travelers' testimony (21:29) that the wicked man is spared for the day of calamity (21:30) and even honored at burial: וְ֭הוּא לִקְבָר֣וֹת יוּבָ֑ל “Yet he will be borne to the grave.” web:Job.21.32. The chapter closes on the same root with which it opened — וְ֭אֵיךְ תְּנַחֲמ֣וּנִי הָ֑בֶל “So how can you comfort me with nonsense” web:Job.21.34 answers “Let this be your consolation.” web:Job.21.2, תְּנַחֲמ֣וּנִי echoing תַּנְח֥וּמֹֽתֵיכֶֽם — turning the friends' own opening request back on them as a rebuke. A SAMEKH follows 21:34 (oshb:Job.21.34 (setumah, single-witness)), corroborating the close of Job's reply immediately before Eliphaz's third-speech formula opens at 22:1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 21:32-34 as its own decision would separate the burial-honor image from the accusation it is answering.
literature_type_guess: Aging-and-grave-filling despite perpetual wickedness pattern

boundary_rationale: The speaker-change seam at Job.21.1|Job.22.1 opens this row: the previous row closes with Job answering (וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר, oshb:Job.21.1), and this row opens with Eliphaz answering instead (וַ֭יַּעַן אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר, oshb:Job.22.1; “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,” web:Job.22.1). The formula's epithet is spelled defectively here (הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י) against the fuller spelling Eliphaz's first two formula instances carry (הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י, oshb:Job.4.1 and oshb:Job.15.1); swept independently, the defective spelling occurs at Job.22.1 alone (sweep: 1 book-wide) while the fuller spelling occurs 5 times book-wide, both in formula position and in narration (oshb:Job.2.11, oshb:Job.4.1, oshb:Job.15.1, oshb:Job.42.7, oshb:Job.42.9). Four verse-initial ha-interrogative tokens open this row in sequence — הַלְאֵ֥ל (Job.22.2), הַחֵ֣פֶץ (Job.22.3), הֲֽ֭מִיִּרְאָ֣תְךָ (Job.22.4), הֲלֹ֣א (Job.22.5) — the first three of which WEB's own punctuation further unpacks into four question-marked clauses, since Job.22.3's second colon (וְאִם בֶּ֝֗צַע כִּֽי תַתֵּ֥ם דְּרָכֶֽיךָ) is also rendered as a question though it opens on a mid-verse וְאִם rather than a fresh he-token; Job.22.5's הֲלֹ֣א (oshb:Job.22.5) sharpens the charge from piety to outright wickedness, setting up the itemized list that follows without yet stating it. Eliphaz's fifth and final ha-interrogative in this speech falls outside this row, at Job.22.12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at Job.22.4 and treating Job.22.5 as an opening line of the accusation catalogue was rejected, since Job.22.5 is still framed as an interrogative continuing the ha-prefixed question series of Job.22.2-Job.22.4, against the declarative register the catalogue itself uses from Job.22.6 on — a register contrast, not an asyndetic one: three of the catalogue's six verses (Job.22.6, Job.22.8, Job.22.11) open on overt connectives (כִּֽי, וְאִ֣ישׁ, אוֹ) rather than asyndetically, Job.22.6 itself a subordinating ki-clause.
literature_type_guess: Eliphaz's third-cycle response opening with piety-premise

boundary_rationale: The itemized accusation opens with an asyndetic ki-clause, כִּֽי (oshb:Job.22.6, “For you have taken pledges from your brother for nothing” web:Job.22.6), listing specific social wrongs charged directly against the addressee in the second person — withheld water and bread, web:Job.22.7 (תַּשְׁקֶ֑ה/תִּֽמְנַֽע, both 2ms) — interrupted at Job.22.8 by a third-person observation with no 2ms form anywhere in it, וְאִ֣ישׁ זְ֭רוֹעַ ל֣וֹ הָאָ֑רֶץ וּנְשׂ֥וּא פָ֝נִ֗ים יֵ֣שֶׁב בָּֽהּ (“But as for the mighty man, he had the earth. The honorable man, he lived in it.” web:Job.22.8), before the 2ms accusatory chain resumes at web:Job.22.9 (widows sent away empty, שִׁלַּ֣חְתָּ, 2ms; orphans' arms broken), before the unit closes with an explicit consequence particle, עַל כֵּ֭ן (oshb:Job.22.10, “Therefore snares are around you” web:Job.22.10), running through the floods-of-water image at Job.22.11. The whole span reads as one grounds-to-result movement: alleged sins, then their supposed effect on the accused.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Job.22.6-Job.22.11 as a mere continuation of the preceding questions rather than its own row was set aside, because the consequence particle at Job.22.10 closes a self-contained list-then-result unit that the interrogative series before it does not share.
literature_type_guess: Indictment catalog Job's concrete social-injustice accusations

boundary_rationale: Eliphaz's fifth ha-interrogative in this speech opens this row — הֲֽלֹא (oshb:Job.22.12, “Isn’t God in the heights of heaven? See the height of the stars, how high they are!” web:Job.22.12), echoing the questioning register of Job.22.5 but turning to a new subject: God's remoteness in the heights of heaven — the second occurrence specifically of the narrower skeleton הלא (Job.22.5 and Job.22.12 share it, differing merely in meteg and cantillation). Eliphaz then puts a quotation in the accused's mouth, מַה יָּ֣דַֽע אֵ֑ל (oshb:Job.22.13), and answers it by describing the old way the wicked of ages past have trodden, who said to God their own words, ס֣וּר מִמֶּ֑נּוּ (oshb:Job.22.17) - a matching direct-quote core that frames the whole unit as one argument about a remote-God theology and its historical champions. The row closes as the righteous mock that generation's ruin at Job.22.19-Job.22.20, before the address shifts to direct imperative appeal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this row into a remoteness-question unit (Job.22.12-Job.22.14) and a separate old-way unit (Job.22.15-Job.22.20) was considered and dropped not for lack of a signal at that seam — Job.22.15 in fact opens on its own interrogative he (הַאֹ֣רַח, patah, distinct from the definite article's qamets at הָאָ֑רֶץ Job.22.8 and הָאֹמְרִ֣ים Job.22.17) and shifts address from the 3ms verbs of Job.22.14 (יִרְאֶ֑ה, יִתְהַלָּֽךְ) to the 2ms תִּשְׁמֹ֑ר — but because the quoted words at Job.22.13 and Job.22.17 answer one another across the whole span, holding Job.22.12-Job.22.20 together as one argument about a remote-God theology and its historical champions despite that interior seam.
literature_type_guess: Darkness theology God's transcendence above starlight

boundary_rationale: Address shifts from third-person description of the wicked to direct second-person imperative: הַסְכֶּן נָ֣א (oshb:Job.22.21, “Acquaint yourself with him now, and be at peace” web:Job.22.21), opening Eliphaz's closing appeal. The conditional particle אִם (oshb:Job.22.23) then sets the return-to-Shaddai protasis whose apodosis promises being built up, and the appeal continues through the treasure-exchange imagery of Job.22.24-Job.22.25 (laying gold in the dust in exchange for Shaddai himself as treasure).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping Job.22.21-Job.22.30 together as one ten-verse appeal was rejected in favor of a split at Job.22.25, though the chain's own consequent clause is already running by that point — וְהָיָ֣ה שַׁדַּ֣י בְּצָרֶ֑יךָ (Job.22.25) is itself a waw-qatal result clause, not a further protasis — and Job.22.26's own consequence particle simply continues that same result movement rather than opening a fresh one, so no clause-type boundary marks Job.22.25|Job.22.26 itself. The appeal's imperative-to-promise register shift (imperative at Job.22.21 and Job.22.23-Job.22.24, promise from Job.22.25 on) in fact falls one verse earlier, inside this row's own span, rather than at its Job.22.25|Job.22.26 close; the retained split is kept as a topical break within the continuous appeal-to-promise material, disclosed as weaker than a fresh clause-type opening.
literature_type_guess: Repentance-formula conditional submission with treasure-speech

boundary_rationale: כִּי אָ֭ז (oshb:Job.22.26, “For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty” web:Job.22.26) continues, rather than reopens, the unbroken veqatal/result chain running from Job.22.23's protasis (אִם תָּשׁ֣וּב עַד שַׁ֭דַּי תִּבָּנֶ֑ה) through Job.22.24's imperative and Job.22.25's own waw-qatal consequent (וְהָיָ֣ה שַׁדַּ֣י בְּצָרֶ֑יךָ); no renewed protasis, address-shift, or formula marks Job.22.25|Job.22.26 itself. This row's material — delight in Shaddai, answered prayer, decreed authority, and rescue for the humble — closes the speech at Job.22.30 on the strength of that continuous chain; the appeal's own imperative-to-promise register shift, disclosed as this row's best available ground, in fact falls one verse earlier, at Job.22.24|Job.22.25 inside the preceding row (as at Job.22.21-Job.22.25), so it continues unbroken across this row's own opening rather than marking it. A petuchah follows Job.22.30 (oshb:Job.22.30 (petuchah, single-witness)), corroborating - at Writings-tier-3 weak strength, not as a driver - a break at the chapter's end, where Job's own vaya'an formula opens the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this row back into Job.22.21-Job.22.25 was declined not because Job.22.26 opens a distinct result movement — the veqatal chain from Job.22.23 runs unbroken through it — but because doing so would erase the petuchah's (single-witness) association with the speech's own genuine closing edge at Job.22.30, and because the register shift from imperative appeal (Job.22.21-Job.22.24) to sustained promise (from Job.22.25 on) still offers a defensible, if weaker, internal seam near this row's own opening.
literature_type_guess: Conditional-blessing formulation with answer-to-prayer certainty

boundary_rationale: Speaker changes again: where Job.22.1 opened Eliphaz's speech, this row opens with Job's own vaya'an, וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.23.1, “Then Job answered,” web:Job.23.1). Job's complaint (Job.23.2) leads into the wish formula מִֽי יִתֵּ֣ן (oshb:Job.23.3, one of 9 verses book-wide carrying this formula, sweep: 9 book-wide), Job's desire to find God's seat and argue his case, set his cause in order, and be heard - a self-contained courtroom fantasy running through Job.23.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the row at Job.23.5 and treating Job.23.6-Job.23.7 as a loosely attached coda was set aside, since those two verses complete the very courtroom scenario Job proposes in Job.23.4-Job.23.5 rather than opening a new topic.
literature_type_guess: Job's fifth-cycle speech opening with seeking-God orientation

boundary_rationale: A presentative particle opens a new movement, הֵ֤ן קֶ֣דֶם (oshb:Job.23.8, “If I go east, he is not there. If I go west, I can’t find him.” web:Job.23.8), the four-direction search that fails to locate God. An adversative כִּֽי (oshb:Job.23.10) then pivots from that failed search to confidence that God nonetheless knows Job's way and will vindicate him like tested gold, and the row closes with Job's claim of fidelity to God's commandment and words at Job.23.11-Job.23.12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking this row at Job.23.9|Job.23.10, separating the failed search from the gold-testing confidence, was tried and dropped as too fine a cut for a five-verse unit whose search-then-trust movement reads as one strophe.
literature_type_guess: Omnidirectional-seeking paradox with trust-finding resolution

boundary_rationale: An adversative opens the row's final movement in chapter 23, וְה֣וּא בְ֭אֶחָד (oshb:Job.23.13, “But he stands alone, and who can oppose him” web:Job.23.13), shifting from Job's fidelity to God's sovereign, uncontested freedom to do as he pleases, and Job's resulting terror at his presence (Job.23.15-Job.23.17). No new speech formula divides Job.23.17 from Job.24.1; the row's close instead rests on the topic turn at the interrogative opening Job.24.1 (מַדּ֗וּעַ, oshb:Job.24.1), which moves from Job's own terror to a general complaint about the fate of the oppressed - a different subject and a different grammatical person (the world's wronged, not Job's own encounter with God).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Letting this row run past the chapter break into Job.24.1-Job.24.4, since no vaya'an or vayosef intervenes there, was rejected because Job.24.1's own interrogative opens a genuinely different subject rather than continuing Job's account of his own terror.
literature_type_guess: Divine-purpose fixity with appointed-path and gold-testing

boundary_rationale: This row opens with the interrogative מַדּ֗וּעַ (oshb:Job.24.1, “Why aren’t times laid up by the Almighty? Why don’t those who know him see his days?” web:Job.24.1), asking why Shaddai reserves no days of reckoning, then names an opening class of oppressors: those who move landmarks, seize flocks, drive off the fatherless's donkey, and take the widow's ox in pledge, ending with the needy turned aside and the poor hiding themselves at Job.24.4.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this row together with Job.24.5-Job.24.12 into one twelve-verse catalogue was considered, but the presentative particle opening Job.24.5 marks a real shift from listing oppressors' acts to picturing the victims' own daily struggle, worth its own row.
literature_type_guess: Landmark-moving oppressors opening the complaint

boundary_rationale: A presentative particle opens this row, הֵ֤ן פְּרָאִ֨ים (oshb:Job.24.5, “Behold, as wild donkeys in the desert, they go out to their work, seeking diligently for food. The wilderness yields them bread for their children.” web:Job.24.5), turning from the oppressors' acts to the poor's own struggle for food like wild donkeys in the wilderness, then back to further wrongs done to them (fatherless plucked from the breast, the naked carrying sheaves, treading presses while thirsty). The unit closes on a summarizing clause, וֶ֝אֱל֗וֹהַּ לֹא יָשִׂ֥ים תִּפְלָֽה (oshb:Job.24.12, “yet God doesn’t regard the folly” web:Job.24.12) - answering the opening why-does-Shaddai-not-act question of Job.24.1 in kind, even though the two verses do not share a fixed refrain.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting this row at Job.24.8|Job.24.9 to separate the wilderness imagery from the renewed list of wrongs was tried and abandoned: verse-initial words across Job.24.5-Job.24.12 are 0-of-8 waw-initial (הן / בשדה / ערום / מזרם / יגזלו / ערום / בין / מעיר), so no conjunction marks that seam either way. What sits at Job.24.8|Job.24.9 is an unmarked reversal of grammatical participant -- victims (Job.24.5-Job.24.8) give way to their oppressors (יגזלו, Job.24.9, bare 3mp yiqtol) -- with the subject left unexpressed on both sides, short of an explicit participant or address shift; that reversal is texture inside one list, not a tier-1 seam.
literature_type_guess: Poor's wilderness foraging amid material deprivation

boundary_rationale: A class-naming formula opens this row, הֵ֤מָּה הָיוּ֮ בְּֽמֹרְדֵ֫י א֥וֹר (oshb:Job.24.13, “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths.” web:Job.24.13), introducing a distinct set of wrongdoers - the murderer, the adulterer, and the housebreaker - who operate by night and shun the light, closing with the terror of thick darkness at Job.24.17. The row itself is a coherent criminals-of-the-dark unit, but the material immediately after it (from Job.24.18) shifts register in a way this row does not itself extend into and does not attempt to resolve.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this row through Job.24.24 as one long unit covering both the criminals-of-the-dark material and the perishing imagery after it was rejected, since Job.24.13's naming formula marks a class distinct from what follows, even where the material after it grows harder to place with confidence.
literature_type_guess: Criminals operating under cover of night darkness

boundary_rationale: This row opens with קַֽל ה֤וּא (oshb:Job.24.18, “They are foam on the surface of the waters. Their portion is cursed in the earth. They don’t turn into the way of the vineyards.” web:Job.24.18), describing the wicked as foam swept away and their portion cursed, running through Job.24.21's barren-widow imagery, then turns with וּמָשַׁ֣ךְ אַבִּירִ֣ים (oshb:Job.24.22, “Yet God preserves the mighty by his power” web:Job.24.22) to describe those same figures secured and watched over. No vaya'an, vayosef, address shift, or scene marker interrupts the MT between Job.24.17 and Job.24.24; the row is chunked as one continuous span for that reason, held rather than resolved. A register-based rival reading exists and is recorded, not adopted: some hear Job.24.18-Job.24.21's swift-perishing language as Job's own citation or ventriloquism of the friends' retribution doctrine (in tension with his complaint at Job.24.1 that Shaddai reserves no such days), rather than as Job's settled claim; the MT gives no formula or address-shift marker inside this span to decide between that rival and a straightforward reading, and no source-critical rearrangement is invoked to settle it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this row at Job.24.21|Job.24.22 to separate the perishing description from the God-preserves turn was drafted and then dropped, because imposing a division there would assert a resolution to the passage's disputed register that no MT marker actually signals.
literature_type_guess: Wicked's perishing and preservation register tension

boundary_rationale: This closing part-seam row shifts to Job's own 1cs voice after the third-person wicked material that precedes it: וְאִם לֹ֣א אֵ֭פוֹ מִ֣י יַכְזִיבֵ֑נִי וְיָשֵׂ֥ם לְ֝אַ֗ל מִלָּתִֽי (oshb:Job.24.25, “If it isn’t so now, who will prove me a liar, and make my speech worth nothing?” web:Job.24.25), the interrogative מִ֣י carrying the challenge on the 1cs-suffixed יַכְזִיבֵ֑נִי and מִלָּתִֽי -- a legal-challenge formula that is a book-wide singleton (skeleton sweep: 1 book-wide for the two-word string) -- closing Job's whole reply before Bildad's own vaya'an opens the next part at Job.25.1 (“Then Bildad the Shuhite answered,” web:Job.25.1). A setumah follows Job.24.25 (oshb:Job.24.25 (setumah, single-witness)), corroborating -- at Writings-tier-3 weak strength -- a break exactly where the speech itself ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this closing challenge back into the Job.24.18-Job.24.24 row was declined, since the return to Job's own direct address ('who will prove me a liar') is a distinct voice shift from the third-person description before it, and the setumah mark's (single-witness) association with a genuine edge would otherwise be lost.
literature_type_guess: Job's legal challenge daring proof of false speech

boundary_rationale: Bildad's third reply opens with the vaya'an formula, וַ֭יַּעַן בִּלְדַּ֥ד הַשֻּׁחִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.25.1) -- spelled defectively (no medial vav), matching his second-cycle form and distinct from the fuller spelling at oshb:Job.8.1 (sweep: 2 book-wide for the defective spelling, skeleton tier: oshb:Job.18.1, oshb:Job.25.1). The formula opens straight into a doxology on divine dominion: “Dominion and fear are with him. He makes peace in his high places” (web:Job.25.2) and “Can his armies be counted? On whom does his light not arise?” (web:Job.25.3) -- a self-answering rhetorical question, הֲיֵ֣שׁ מִ֭סְפָּר... (oshb:Job.25.3), that closes the row before Bildad turns to a harsher question about human standing.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping Bildad's whole six-verse reply as one undivided strophe instead of separating the opening doxology from the question it sets up.
literature_type_guess: Bildad's dominion doxology exalting divine majesty

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative opens the row: “How then can man be just with God? Or how can he who is born of a woman be clean?” (web:Job.25.4), rendering וּמַה יִּצְדַּ֣ק אֱנ֣וֹשׁ עִם אֵ֑ל... (oshb:Job.25.4). The question presses by a fortiori comparison -- even the moon and stars lack purity in his sight (web:Job.25.5; הֵ֣ן עַד יָ֭רֵחַ וְלֹ֣א יַאֲהִ֑יל..., oshb:Job.25.5) -- before collapsing onto humanity: “How much less man, who is a worm, and the son of man, who is a worm!” (web:Job.25.6; אַ֭ף כִּֽי אֱנ֣וֹשׁ רִמָּ֑ה וּבֶן אָ֝דָ֗ם תּוֹלֵעָֽה, oshb:Job.25.6). A PE mark follows in the single-witness inventory (oshb:Job.25.6 (petuchah, single-witness)), and the vaya'an formula opens Job's reply at web:Job.26.1, so this row's close carries two independent kinds of corroboration even though the interrogative alone marks its own opening.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this a fortiori turn back into the opening doxology rather than treating Bildad's six verses as two strophes.
literature_type_guess: Purity argument descending from moon-stars to worms

boundary_rationale: Job's reply opens with the vaya'an formula, וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.26.1) -- the MT frame this row and the rest of the part follow through the third-cycle disarray of chapters 25-28. A PE mark precedes this opening, following Bildad's own close at Job.25.6 (oshb:Job.25.6 (petuchah, single-witness)). What follows is direct, second-person sarcasm aimed at Bildad: “How have you helped him who is without power! How have you saved the arm that has no strength!” (web:Job.26.2; מֶה עָזַ֥רְתָּ לְלֹא כֹ֑חַ ה֝וֹשַׁ֗עְתָּ זְר֣וֹעַ לֹא עֹֽז, oshb:Job.26.2) and “To whom have you uttered words? Whose spirit came out of you?” (web:Job.26.4; אֶת מִ֭י הִגַּ֣דְתָּ מִלִּ֑ין וְנִשְׁמַת מִ֝י יָצְאָ֥ה מִמֶּֽךָּ, oshb:Job.26.4). The finite verbs addressed to Bildad in Job.26.2-Job.26.4a are second-person (עָזַ֥רְתָּ, ה֝וֹשַׁ֗עְתָּ, יָּ֭עַצְתָּ, הוֹדָֽעְתָּ, הִגַּ֣דְתָּ); the frame verbs of Job.26.1 are third-person wayyiqtols, and the relative clause of Job.26.4b (יָצְאָ֥ה, agreeing with its interrogative subject) is third-person feminine, with just the trailing מִמֶּֽךָּ carrying second person. The direct address to Bildad ends at Job.26.4, before the person shift to third-person cosmology at Job.26.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending Job's direct rebuke of Bildad through verse 14 instead of marking a shift at the person change to third-person cosmology at Job.26.5.
literature_type_guess: Job's sarcastic rebuke addressing Bildad directly

boundary_rationale: The address shifts from second-person rebuke to a third-person catalog of God's cosmic power: the departed spirits beneath the waters (web:Job.26.5; הָרְפָאִ֥ים יְחוֹלָ֑לוּ מִתַּ֥חַת מַ֝֗יִם וְשֹׁכְנֵיהֶֽם, oshb:Job.26.5), Sheol and Abaddon uncovered before him (web:Job.26.6; עָר֣וֹם שְׁא֣וֹל נֶגְדּ֑וֹ וְאֵ֥ין כְּ֝ס֗וּת לָֽאֲבַדּֽוֹן, oshb:Job.26.6), the sea stirred by his power and Rahab struck through by his understanding (web:Job.26.12; בְּ֭כֹחוֹ רָגַ֣ע הַיָּ֑ם ובתובנתו וּ֝בִתְבוּנָת֗וֹ מָ֣חַץ רָֽהַב, oshb:Job.26.12 -- a ketiv/qere pair sits inside this verse, single-witness disclosure), then the heavens garnished and his hand piercing the fleeing serpent (web:Job.26.13; בְּ֭רוּחוֹ שָׁמַ֣יִם שִׁפְרָ֑ה חֹֽלֲלָ֥ה יָ֝ד֗וֹ נָחָ֥שׁ בָּרִֽיחַ, oshb:Job.26.13). The catalog closes on a gnomic reflection: “Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways. How small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?” (web:Job.26.14; הֶן אֵ֤לֶּה קְצ֬וֹת... מִ֣י יִתְבּוֹנָֽן, oshb:Job.26.14). Two further ketiv/qere pairs (his way/his ways; his power/his mighty acts) sit inside this closing verse (single-witness disclosure: oshb:Job.26.14), and a SAMEKH mark follows it in the same inventory (oshb:Job.26.14 (setumah, single-witness)). This row out-argues the very dominion doxology Bildad opened with at web:Job.25.2-Job.25.3, at five times the length.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attributing this cosmological catalog to Bildad's developing argument rather than to Job's ironic escalation of it.
literature_type_guess: God's cosmological power catalog ending whisper-saying

boundary_rationale: Job's mashal resumption opens with the vayosef formula, וַיֹּ֣סֶף אִ֭יּוֹב שְׂאֵ֥ת מְשָׁל֗וֹ וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.27.1) -- the same wording, byte-for-byte, that reopens at web:Job.29.1 after the wisdom poem (sweep: 2 book-wide for this exact formula, byte tier: oshb:Job.27.1, oshb:Job.29.1), and per the MT frame this span governs everything through the end of chapter 28. The formula opens an oath of personal integrity: “As God lives, who has taken away my right, the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter” (web:Job.27.2; חַי אֵ֭ל הֵסִ֣יר מִשְׁפָּטִ֑י וְ֝שַׁדַּ֗י הֵמַ֥ר נַפְשִֽׁי, oshb:Job.27.2), closing “Far be it from me that I should justify you. Until I die I will not put away my integrity from me” (web:Job.27.5; חָלִ֣ילָה לִּי֮ אִם אַצְדִּ֪יק אֶ֫תְכֶ֥ם..., oshb:Job.27.5). Chapter 27 itself carries no PE or SAMEKH mark in the single-witness inventory -- a SAMEKH mark precedes this row's own opening, following Job.26.14 (setumah, single-witness), the mark closing the preceding cosmological catalog immediately before this oath begins -- so this row's internal edges rest on the formula and the oath's own asseverative particles rather than on mark corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the oath at the parenthetical aside in verse 3 instead of reading 27:1-6 as one continuous asseveration.
literature_type_guess: Job's self-imprecatory oath of personal integrity

boundary_rationale: The oath's register turns from asseveration to imprecation: “Let my enemy be as the wicked. Let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous” (web:Job.27.7; יְהִ֣י כְ֭רָשָׁע אֹ֣יְבִ֑י וּמִתְקוֹמְמִ֥י כְעַוָּֽל, oshb:Job.27.7), then to a question about that wicked one's standing: “For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?” (web:Job.27.8; כִּ֤י מַה תִּקְוַ֣ת חָ֭נֵף..., oshb:Job.27.8). The row closes turning back on the friends themselves: “Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?” (web:Job.27.12; הֵן אַתֶּ֣ם כֻּלְּכֶ֣ם חֲזִיתֶ֑ם וְלָמָּה זֶּ֝֗ה הֶ֣בֶל תֶּהְבָּֽלוּ, oshb:Job.27.12) -- a second-person plural rebuke closing the ring opened by the second-person singular taunt against Bildad at web:Job.26.2.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading verses 7-12 as a continuation of the personal-integrity oath rather than as its own imprecatory turn. Separately, a live rival at the row's own back edge is recorded, not adopted: oshb:Job.27.11's אוֹרֶ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֣ם (“I will teach you”, web:Job.27.11) is the earliest second-person-plural address after Job.27.5 -- the 2mp object pronoun אֶתְכֶ֣ם sweeps 6 book-wide at skeleton tier (Job.13.9, Job.13.10, Job.13.11, Job.27.5, Job.27.11, Job.32.6), with Job.27.5 and Job.27.11 the members inside this mashal -- so Job.27.11-Job.27.12's direct teaching address to the friends could instead be read as the hinge introducing the deictic heading of Job.27.13 rather than as this row's own closing turn. The row's edge at Job.27.12|Job.27.13 stands on the independently attested heading formula at Job.27.13 (a two-word deictic opening, byte-identical to oshb:Job.20.29, sweep: 2 book-wide, with a shared second-colon echo וְֽנַחֲלַ֥ת sweeping 3 book-wide (skeleton tier) -- Job.20.29, Job.27.13, Job.31.2; at byte/accent-stripped tier the count narrows to 2, Job.27.13 and Job.31.2 alone sharing this pointed spelling with meteg and merkha, while Job.20.29 carries the distinct accent-stripped form וְנַחֲלַ֖ת, meteg-less with tipeha), so the rival at Job.27.10|Job.27.11 is disclosed rather than adopted.
literature_type_guess: Imprecation turning to the godless's own destruction

boundary_rationale: A deictic heading opens the row's final movement: “This is the portion of a wicked man with God, the heritage of oppressors, which they receive from the Almighty” (web:Job.27.13; זֶ֤ה חֵֽלֶק אָדָ֖ם רָשָׁ֥ע עִם אֵ֑ל וְֽנַחֲלַ֥ת עָ֝רִיצִ֗ים מִשַּׁדַּ֥י יִקָּֽחוּ, oshb:Job.27.13) -- a verse carrying two paseq segs in the single-witness seg layer (oshb:Job.27.13 (paseq, single-witness)). The two-word deictic opening זֶ֤ה חֵֽלֶק is byte-identical to the closing verse of Zophar's second speech, oshb:Job.20.29 (זֶ֤ה חֵֽלֶק אָדָ֣ם רָ֭שָׁע מֵאֱלֹהִ֑ים וְנַחֲלַ֖ת אִמְר֣וֹ מֵאֵֽל, web:Job.20.29 “This is the portion of a wicked man from God, the heritage appointed to him by God”) -- sweep: 2 book-wide at byte tier, the object's only two members -- and the parallel continues into the second colon, where both verses open with וְֽנַחֲלַ֥ת (skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide, adding Job.31.2). What follows catalogs that wicked man's ruin -- children, wealth, house, and life all swept away -- closing “Men will clap their hands at him, and will hiss him out of his place” (web:Job.27.23; יִשְׂפֹּ֣ק עָלֵ֣ימוֹ כַפֵּ֑ימוֹ וְיִשְׁרֹ֥ק עָ֝לָ֗יו מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ, oshb:Job.27.23). The register here is close to the wicked-man's-doom catalog Zophar built his second speech around, and the byte-twinned heading strengthens that reading as more than a loose thematic echo; yet the MT text carries no new speech formula at this seam -- the material stays inside Job's vayosef mashal from web:Job.27.1 rather than being reassigned to a friend.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating verses 13-23 as displaced Zophar material and re-attributing them outside the vayosef frame.
literature_type_guess: Wicked man's comprehensive ruin from wealth grave

boundary_rationale: No new speech formula opens chapter 28: the particle כִּ֤י יֵ֣שׁ ('surely there is', asseverative, oshb:Job.28.1) begins a mining excursus inside the same vayosef span that opened at web:Job.27.1, describing how miners break shafts for silver and gold “away from where people live” (web:Job.28.4). The row runs through techniques for extracting hidden treasure -- “He puts his hand on the flinty rock, and he overturns the mountains by the roots” (web:Job.28.9) -- closing “He binds the streams that they don't trickle. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light” (web:Job.28.11; מִ֭בְּכִי נְהָר֣וֹת חִבֵּ֑שׁ וְ֝תַעֲלֻמָ֗הּ יֹ֣צִא אֽוֹר, oshb:Job.28.11). A PE mark follows in the single-witness inventory (oshb:Job.28.11 (petuchah, single-witness)), and two paseq segs mark verses 3 and 4 within the row (oshb:Job.28.3 (paseq, single-witness); oshb:Job.28.4 (paseq, single-witness)).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Marking a new top-level unit at 28:1 despite the absence of any speech-formula seam there.
literature_type_guess: Mining catalog seeking silver hidden underground

boundary_rationale: The wisdom poem's refrain opens the row at its earlier of two book-wide occurrences (sweep: 2 book-wide, skeleton tier: oshb:Job.28.12, oshb:Job.28.20): “But where will wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?” (web:Job.28.12; וְֽ֭הַחָכְמָה מֵאַ֣יִן תִּמָּצֵ֑א וְאֵ֥י זֶ֝ה מְק֣וֹם בִּינָֽה, oshb:Job.28.12) -- the fronted, topicalized 'wisdom' breaking from the mining catalog's third-person miner-subject. What follows argues wisdom's price is beyond purchase: “It can't be gotten for gold, neither will silver be weighed for its price” (web:Job.28.15; לֹא יֻתַּ֣ן סְג֣וֹר תַּחְתֶּ֑יהָ..., oshb:Job.28.15), running through onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, and topaz before closing “The topaz of Ethiopia will not equal it. It won't be valued with pure gold” (web:Job.28.19). A PE mark follows in the single-witness inventory (oshb:Job.28.19 (petuchah, single-witness)), immediately before the refrain's second occurrence reopens the question in the row that follows (oshb:Job.28.20); another PE mark already precedes this row's own opening, following Job.28.11 (petuchah, single-witness), the mark closing the preceding mining excursus immediately before this price catalog begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the price catalog together with the preceding mining excursus as one long row instead of opening a new strophe at the refrain.
literature_type_guess: Where-wisdom-found refrain opening unpurchasable-price panel

boundary_rationale: The refrain's second book-wide occurrence (sweep: 2 book-wide, skeleton tier: oshb:Job.28.12, oshb:Job.28.20) reopens the question with a varied verb: “Where then does wisdom come from? Where is the place of understanding?” (web:Job.28.20; וְֽ֭הַחָכְמָה מֵאַ֣יִן תָּב֑וֹא וְאֵ֥י זֶ֝֗ה מְק֣וֹם בִּינָֽה, oshb:Job.28.20) -- the verb replacing the earlier occurrence's verb at web:Job.28.12. A PE mark (single-witness) precedes this opening, following the price catalog's own close at Job.28.19 (oshb:Job.28.19 (petuchah, single-witness)). Even the underworld knows wisdom merely by rumor: “Destruction and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.’” (web:Job.28.22; אֲבַדּ֣וֹן וָ֭מָוֶת אָ֣מְר֑וּ..., oshb:Job.28.22), echoing the Abaddon of web:Job.26.6. The row then turns to God's exclusive access, opening with the general divine name (אֱ֭לֹהִים, bare word-token sweep: 11 verses book-wide -- Job.1.1, Job.1.5, Job.1.8, Job.1.9, Job.1.16, Job.2.3, Job.2.9, Job.5.8, Job.28.23, Job.34.9, Job.38.7) rather than the dialogue's usual Eloah (bare sweep: 37 verses book-wide) or Shaddai (bare sweep: 23 verses book-wide): “God understands its way, and he knows its place” (web:Job.28.23; אֱ֭לֹהִים הֵבִ֣ין דַּרְכָּ֑הּ..., oshb:Job.28.23) -- inside this mashal, Eloah names God at Job.27.3/Job.27.8/Job.27.10 and Shaddai at Job.27.2/Job.27.10/Job.27.11, against the general name's one use here at Job.28.23. The row closes on a chain of four verbs of discovery: “then he saw it, and declared it. He established it, yes, and searched it out” (web:Job.28.27; אָ֣ז רָ֭אָהּ וַֽיְסַפְּרָ֑הּ הֱ֝כִינָ֗הּ וְגַם חֲקָרָֽהּ, oshb:Job.28.27). The verse-initial name shift at Job.28.23 sits four verses inside this row's own span rather than at either edge -- it is disclosed here as texture inside the row, not as a driver, since it argues across the row's own interior (toward a possible Job.28.20-Job.28.22 / Job.28.23-Job.28.27 split) rather than at either boundary the row actually draws.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the hidden-from-creation lines from the God's-exclusive-knowledge lines into two separate rows instead of reading 20-27 as one strophe.
literature_type_guess: Wisdom hidden from creation yet known to God

boundary_rationale: A quotation frame closes the poem: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָֽאָדָ֗ם הֵ֤ן יִרְאַ֣ת אֲ֭דֹנָי הִ֣יא חָכְמָ֑ה וְס֖וּר מֵרָ֣ע בִּינָֽה (oshb:Job.28.28), rendered “To man he said, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’” (web:Job.28.28). This is one of nine frame vayomer tokens book-wide (sweep: 9 book-wide, per-family count), and the only one that names its addressee as the generic 'to man' rather than fronting a subject name -- a construction closer to the addressee-marked frame at web:Job.2.10 ('to her') than to the six subject-fronted frames of the prose prologue, or to the subjectless exclamation at web:Job.1.21.
